speechtext: I observe that my hon. friend's resolution states, "in accordance with the usual practice." For what particular reason should we remit these fees?
The matter was discussed in committee this morning, and the resolution was adopted by the committee. I would ask the chairman of the committee to explain the matter.

The main reason for the recommendation of the committee that these fines be refunded is that the lawyers engaged in these cases did not file their petitions before the House of Commons in due time, while the petitions were filed with the Senate on time. With the rules as they are at present the difficulty is this: In the Senate I believe they have at least twelve weeks within which to present their petitions, while in the House of Commons they have only six weeks. This has resulted in confusion and embarrassment for the lawyers engaged in these cases, and some of them have been one day late, and others two or three days late in presenting their

petitions, rendering the parties liable to a fine of $200. In the particular cases that came before the committee this morning we concluded that under the circumstances the usual practice should be followed and these fines refunded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are fines?

Yes. Having had a little experience in presiding over this committee, I very much feel like recommending that some procedure be adopted which would obviate cases of this kind coming before us, because one would expect that the lawyers in these cases at least should know the period within which the petitions should be filed in both houses. If the time for receiving the petitions were the same for both houses, it would obviate such cases as we have had to consider lately.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
On April 23 last I asked the
Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) a question respecting the Quebec, Saguenay and Ghibougamau railway, and he was to obtain if possible certain further information. I have clipped from a newspaper a prospectus of the issue of the bonds of the company and a reading notice that:
The company has an arrangement with the Canadian National Railways under which the latter company will approve the location of line as well as supervise its construction. The company has also a close understanding with the Canadian National Railways with respect to the handling and development of traffic.
Certain officers of the Canadian National are directors of the enterprise, and having in mind what transpired in connection with Grand Trunk Pacific obligations, which purchasers in Britain afterwards alleged constituted a debt of this country, I direct the minister's attention to the matter for the purpose of asking him whether the government as such is taking any part in it. A correspondent of mine, who has no political interest in the matter, felt that it might involve us in the same situation as we were involved in with respect to Grand Trunk Pacific obligations, about which the minister is so well aware.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Since the last
occasion on which the matter was mentioned in the house, an official statement has been published by authority of the legal vicepresident of the Canadian National Railways, setting out very clearly the relationship between the Canadian National Railways and the Quebec, Saguenay and Chibougamau Railway. I am also advised by the president that it is correct that the Canadian National is undertaking to approve the route to be followed by the proposed line; is undertaking to supervise standards of construction; and intends to get into a position, with respect to the Quebec, Saguenay and Chibougamau Railway, whereby that railway may not sell its undertaking to any other railway company without first giving the Canadian National an opportunity to purchase it. Further, I am advised that a traffic agreement along the usual lines is in process of negotiation between the Canadian National and the Quebec, Saguenay and Chibougamau Railway, and the president and board of directors of ' the Canadian National deemed it wise, in protecting the interests of the Canadian National, that that company should have representation on the board of the Quebec, Saguenay and Chibougamau Railway Company. There is no financial responsibility, either by the Canadian National or by the government of Canada, for any of the securities issued by the Quebec, Saguenay and Chibougamau Railway Company.
I will discuss the matter further on the estimates.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
When the house rose I was dealing with a feature of the Duncan report which, as I pointed out to the house, perhaps had not received the attention it deserved; I was referring to that portion of the report recommending the renewal of a subvention on coal carried all-rail from the maritime provinces to upper Canada. I was pointing out that on March 30 the government passed an order in council which, as I suggested, had gone further than the recommendation of the commission. My reasons for so stating are two: First, under the old order in council the maximum subvention was 50 cents per ton on coal moving from the maritime provinces. Under the new order in council, whereas the rate was $3.80 per ton the order in council provides that the maximum rate shall be $3 per ton; in other words, instead of a maximum reduction of 50 cents per ton the maximum reduction is 80 cents per ton. Just
in that connection I might say that the new rate is based on the rate provided in the order in council relating to Alberta coal, and therefore the province of Nova Scotia gets the benefit of the Alberta rate under this new order in council. I would also remind the house that the 80 cent reduction is made on a rate which had been already reduced by almost 20 per cent under the Maritime Freight Rates Act of last year. In the province of New Brunswick the rate is reduced from $2.60 to $2.10, a 50 cent reduction.
In still another particular the order in council goes further than the old provision. Under the old order in council provision was made for the transportation by rail to upper Canada from Montreal, of maritime province coal, which had been water borne from Nova Scotia to Montreal. The provision then made called for a reduction of one-fifth of one cent per ton mile, but the maximum subvention which could be made was 50 cents per ton. Under the new order in council that maximum subvention has been increased to 75 cents per ton, which enables Nova Scotia coal to be moved just that much further into the province of Ontario. I call that to the attention of my hon. friends who suggest that this report is not being implemented, and those who will presumably support the amendment which states that the government have refused to implement the recommendations of the commission.
The order in council provides one further feature which is not contained in the original order in council, and that is an inquiry by the Board of Railway Commissioners into the cost of the transportation of coal from Montreal to western Ontario. Those are the benefits which are received by the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in connection with the recommendations made by the Duncan commission for a subvention on maritime coal.
There is still a further point to be considered in connection with coal, because this amendment speaks of coal particularly. The Duncan report contains a recommendation that provision be made for the establishment of coking plants; I would direct the attention of the house to this recommendation, which is on page 36 of the report and which recommends that we proceed without delay to put in practical shape the policy which was recommended so definitely by the Dominion fuel board as the only method by which eastern and central Canada can be relieved of dependence upon imported anthractite. I want to point out that the recommendation of the Dominion fuel board was submitted to the parliamentary committee in 1926; on that recommendation a resolution was drafted

Steel Industry-Mr. Ralston
providing that a subsidy of 3 per cent per year should be paid on coking plants erected for the purpose of using Canadian coal, and that 3 per cent was to cover a period of fifteen years. I want to point out to my hon. friends who fear that this report has not been implemented that the legislation passed last year provided for a subsidy of 4 per cent to private companies, as against the 3 per cent recommended by the Dominion fuel board and 5 per cent to municipal corporations, and that that subsidy permitted the use of 30 per cent of American coal if that were found necessary in order to make a satisfactory coke. It was thought that possibly the requirement of one hundred per cent Canadian coal might defeat the erection of these plants, and it was determined to make the legislation practical. Again, in that respect, the government have gone further than the recommendations of the Duncan commission.
With respect to the duty on coal, we have the authority of my hon. friend who moved this amendment who has already stated his conviction that there is not much chance of an increase in the duty on coal. I do not know whether he has said that in this house, 'but he made that statement in his own county; he has been frank and fair enough to say so. Any special questions of tariff affecting coal are now before the tariff advisory board, as has been stated.
I would mention just two other matters dealt with in the Duncan report; first port development and export trade. I can only mention these matters in passing in order to register the fact that the government have fully carried out the recommendations of the commission. The Duncan commission recommended that statutory harbour commissions be established for the ports of Halifax and St. John. Some time ago attempts were made in this house to show that this meant some sort of special harbour commission different from the commissions existing throughout Canada. I think this house was convinced that the Duncan commission meant exactly what it recommended, a statutory commission based on those commissions whose work they had already investigated, particularly the harbour commission of Montreal. The statutory harbour commissions were established, and this year this house passed votes of $500,000 for the port of Halifax and $5,000,000 for the port of St. John, covering three years, in order that these harbour commissions may function.
Then we come to the question of fisheries. It was recommended that a deputy minister of fisheries be appointed; last session legislation was brought down and placed upon the statute books, in connection with that very 
matter. In addition to that, although it is not recommended in the Duncan report, last fall this government promptly appointed a commission because of an acute condition which arose in connection with the fisheries, and that commission investigated the fisheries of the maritime provinces. As has been stated in this house to-day, the report of that commission was laid on the table only about ten days ago, so I think we can fairly claim that the government have substantially not only carried out the recommendations of the Duncan report but in this case as well have gone even further.
I see I have only a moment or two left, but before I conclude I want to say that my good friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) quoted from an old, well-worn set of statistics with regard to blast furnaces. Those statistics were quoted by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) during the 'budget debate this year. He attempted to show that the blast furnace industry had been going down in this country. I want to remind him and the house that my hon. friend was very careful not to note that two periods of government were covered by the figures which he quoted. He quoted the activities of the blast furnaces in 1913 and then jumped to 1925. In 1913 the men employed in blast furnace operations numbered 1,589, but in 1921, after eight years of rule by his own party, the number had diminished to 614. Since that time there has been a continual increase in this figure, and in 1927 the number of men engaged in operation of blast furnaces was 734.
Let me remind my hon. friend that the output of the blast furnaces in 1913 was about 1,000,000 tons; in 1921 it had gone down to 593,000 tons, and since that time, under this government, it has increased from 593,000 tons to 907,000 tons. The adverse balance of trade in connection with the steel industry was $101,000,000 in 1913; in 1921 it had gone up to $169,000,000 and in 1927 it was back to about $106,000 000.
There was mention made of the town of Trenton. I do not propose to make any parade of what I have been able to do, or what I have been trying to do, but I think when the record is examined it will be found that I have been just as sincere a friend of Trenton as any of the gentlemen on the other side of the house. I have spent a good deal of time and put forth a good deal of effort in order to assist, if I possibly could, in connection with the development and the progress of the steel industry at Trenton.

Steel Industry-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
The Eastern Chronicle had an editorial only a day or two ago which said this about Trenton:
Trenton is busy and likely to be for this year.
I quite realize that the steel industry of Trenton has had a hard time, and also that the mining industry' has had a difficult time, but I say that a very sincere attempt has been made, not always by the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house, to bring about a better situation there. I do not believe, and 1 do not want this house to believe, that the sentiments expressed by my hon. friends represent the sentiment of the people of Nova Scotia.

You
found that out in 1925-26.

My hon. friend found
out a few things too in 1925-26. The people of Nova Scotia understand the situation with regard to the steel and coal industry and they know consideration will be given to these matters just as soon as conditions make it possible and practicable. They know that the matter of freight rates has been effectively dealt with in the way in which the Minister of Railways showed last night. They know that the government has gone much farther in connection with freight rates than was suggested in the Duncan report; that the increases in subsidies have been paid, as recommended by the Dunoan report, yes, and perhaps a little ahead of time. They know that subventions on coal rates have been provided for as recommended by the Duncan report. They know that subsidies to coking plants have been provided for at a greater rate than recommended by the Duncan report. They know that harbour commissions have been established, and votes have been made so that they may carry on; that legislation has been passed with respect to a deputy minister of fisheries, and that in connection with this industry there has been the additional feature that a special commission has been appointed and has made its report.
I feel that this house is convinced, and I know the people of Nova Scotia are convinced, that there has been honest, sincere, and effective action not only to implement the letter of the Duncan report but to go even further to meet the needs when the situation demanded.

I will
not detain the house at any great length with the remarks I have to make on this question.
At the outset, I want to take direct issue with the amendment that has been moved by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald). When the amendment says that the house regrets the refusal of the government to implement certain recommendations as contained in the Duncan report, it implies a refusal on the part of the government to do this. That is not a correct interpretation of the case, and I do not agree with it.
My hon. friends on the opposite side of the house, during this debate particularly and in some of the previous debates during this session, have undertaken to outline certain things as being recommended in the Duncan report which are not recommended therein. I do not wish to go over the many recommendations that were made, in order to bear out that statement, as I went into it raither fully in the debate on the address earlier in the session. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has gone into it in detail in this debate, so it is unnecessary for me to go over the ground1 again.
I wish to say a word or two in regard to some statements that have been made as to the province of Prince Edward Island, particularly referring to the transportation system, port developments, and the ferry service between the island and the mainland.
I was pleased to hear the announcement made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) yesterday, that the government had come to the decision that it was necessary to provide for a second car ferry. I am sure that information will meet with the approval of the people of Prince Edward Island, regardless of party affiliations. Our people all feel that that was the first necessary step to take at this time, in carrying out the recommendations that were made in the Duncan report.
When hon. members say to this house and to the country that the Duncan report recommended a second ear ferry between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, they place a very narrow and short-sighted interpretation upon the recommendations of that report. The report did not actually recommend a second car ferry, and I will read the recommendations that were made in order that the house and the country may properly grasp the facts.
The Duncan report as we all know was a very able, well considered and well written document. It is a report that will be in our hands for many years to come. I think every member of that commission gave a degree

Steel Industry-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
of consideration to the questions submitted to them that is very rarely given by commissions, and I say that without any reflection on other commissions.
The commission first pointed out that the ferry service was unsatisfactory, and that the railway administration admitted that there was need for supplemental provision being made, either in the form of a second ferry boat or a special freight boat. That was cited by the commission as the opinion of the railway management, and then the commission directly recommended as follows:
We recommend that the matter be gone into from the point of view of placing at the disposal of the island such satisfactory means of communication as will ensure as regular and complete a service as can reasonably be made.
When we look at the recommendation that is made in the report, we must come to the conclusion, as fairminded people, that the Duncan commission went into the matter very fully, and that their recommendation was not limited to a single car ferry, or any single instrument that might be used to provide a satisfactory service. It was mudh broader than that. In effect the commission says that it is the duty of Canada to see that the island shall be ensured as regular and complete a service as reasonably can be given. I think that is the spirit of the report, and it is in that spirit that we must approach the question. I am glad to know, as I said before, that the government has come to the conclusion, as many others who are directly interested in the transportation system of the island have done, that at the present time a second car ferry is needed in older to give the ihland the regular service it should have.
I should like to refer to the question of port development. The Minister of Finance cited expenditures that were made for port development in Prince Edward Island. That work was necessary; it was undertaken by the Department of Public Works before the Duncan commission made its report and the report did not mention directly, just as I said was the case in regard to railways, what was actually needed at the present time in that regard. Let me read that part of the report so that the public may understand the matter. The report states:
We recommend that the Public Works department make an immediate survey of these harbours, particularly as to wharfage and storage accommodation, with a view to adequate provision being made to meet the needs of the island's produce.
To say that we have implemented that recommendation to the full would be saying

too much; but as I said in a previous de-bate

and my remarks have been referred to in the press and in other ways-I think the government have gone as far as they can reasonably be expected to do at thi.3 date towards implementing that recommendation. But it will be seen that the recommendation is a broad one and that it carries with it the statement that the government are responsible for meeting the needs of the island's traffic as time goes on. That I think is understood and I am glad to be able to say that the government were acting toward that end before the recommendation of the commission was tabled in the house.
Let me refer for a moment to what has been said by some other hon. members during the debate regarding certain railway improvements that are necessary on the island. If I may quote from yesterday's Hansard, I find that one of the speakers made this statement:
I was showing how any transportation recommendations in connection with Prince Edward Island had not been carried out, particularly in regard to the standardization of the roadbed, and the ferry steamer.
There is no recommendation in the Duncan report asking for the standardization of the roadbed in Prince Edward Island. That is a narrow interpretation that is being put upon the report. I will not impute any motive to those who put that interpretation on, but it has been used outside of the house in an intent to influence the minds of the electors along a narrow channel. The recommendations of the report are generally for a proper transportation system in the island, not nailing the matter down to any particular action that may be taken at this time, but leaving it open for the future. In that spirit I think the government and the railway department are approaching the matter in an endeavour to carry out the intention of the Duncan commission and the wish of the people.
In the debate yesterday I did not altogether catch what was being said by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) when he was discussing the report with a view to showing the house that what was intended by the Duncan commission had not been sufficiently carried into effect. The main recommendation mentioned in the amendment was that in regard to coal and steel, but it was necessary for my hon. friend to make certain statements regarding the car ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland and the carrying out of certain recommendations in regard to our province, To

Steel Industry-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
do that he read a letter which I find on page 3266 of yesterday's Hansard, and he said that that letter emanated from a responsible citizen in Charlottetown. The hon. member however did not tell the house to whom the letter was addressed or who signed it, and unless he is willing to reveal to the house the author of the letter, I must hold him responsible for the statements made in it. In the last paragraph of that letter the writer uses these words in reference to standardization of the railway:
Those farmers are moreover discriminated against by the expense of an extra handling of their shipments into broad gauge cars.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is willing to tell the house who the author of the letter is. I think the house has a right to know that, and if my hon. friend is not willing to reveal the name of the author he must be responsible for the statements made in the letter. In fairness to the railway management and the transportation system I wish to say that no extra expense to the shipper is involved in the handling of freight or in the transfer of shipments from the narrow gauge railway to the broad gauge railway. The expense of making that transfer is taken care of by the railway and the regular rate on freight is charged on a mileage basis on that part of the line just the same as on any other part. Moreover, as the house well knows, that matter comes under the jurisdiction of the railway commission. These words appear at the close of the quotation:
And yet, John E. Sinclair will say the farmers are satisfied.
I do not know where that quotation was taken from, but so fax as it applies to me I have not used those words either in parliament or in the country. Anything I have to say in regard to the farmers or any other class in Prince Edward Island, I am willing and ready to say in the house or anywhere else, without being quoted in an anonymous letter, the author of which my hon. friend has not seen fit to disclose to the house. Will my hon. friend say by whom and to whom the letter was written? The members are entitled to that information and when he uses the name of an hon. member, it is only fair that the source of his information should be given. If he refuses to give that information, then all I have to say is that he must assume the responsibility for his statement, which as far as it refers to me is not correct.

I described accurately
the gentleman who wrote me the letter. I
have no intention of giving the hon. member any information on that point. I am perfectly willing to accept all responsibility for any statements I make.
Do I understand that the hon. member refuses to say who wrote the letter?

Yes.
Mr. SINCLAIR (Queens). Then I must say that so far as the statement refers to me, it is not correct. I never' made that statement, and if my hon. friend accepts the responsibility for his informant, he must accept my denial and become responsible for a statement that, so far as I am concerned, is not correct.
I thought it was proper that I should make a few remarks on this question, especially in view of what has been said by my hon. friend from Pictou, who has really very little interest in Prince Edward Island unless it is to1 use information of this kind in regard to matters with which he is not familiar himself, and has to take second hand, and in doing so he refuses to divulge the name of his informant. the person to whom the letter was addressed or the person by whom it was signed. Things are getting to a pretty low ebb when my hon. friend has to fall back on such information to support such a motion as we have before us at the present time.
There is nothing further I need say. I could say a good deal as to the effect of the Duncan recommendations in regard to Prince Edward Island, but we have gone thoroughly into that matter on former occasions and I see no necessity for going further into it. I shall only remark that the people of Prince Edward Island without regard to party affiliations will welcome the announcement made in the house last night by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), that the government had come to the decision that it was now time that a second car ferry was provided to carry on the ferry service between the island and the mainland. I agree with the government in their conclusion that this second car ferry is necessary for the service, and it cannot come one minute too soon to meet the increasing necessities of the traffic. During two months of the season that has just passed the business of the ferry was greater than the ferry boats could take care of; that is in the months of November and March, which are the two months when the peak movement of our chief crop, which is potatoes, takes place. With the increased acreage that is now being planted we feel that the present facilities will not be able to handle the traffic

Steel Industry-Mr. Jenkins
this year, and we are glad to know we can hope to have a better service the following year. I am sure that the minister's announcement will be received with the utmost satisfaction by every elector in Prince Edward Island, regardless of party affiliations.

I shall detain the house for only a few moments, but I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to express the appreciation not only of myself but of the people of our province with respect to the announcement made last night by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). Some of our friends of the opposition would have us believe that no attention whatever was being paid by the government to the improvement of our car ferry service, but on looking up the Hansard of last year I find, at page 1336. under date of March 18, 1927, that the Prime Minister made this statement:
A survey of what is required with respect to the needed railway service improvements on Prince Edward Island will, as recommended, be made immediately, in order that future action may be intelligently determined.
The whole matter of ferry boat service between the island and the mainland is now under investigation, as recommended by the commission.
And that investigation has been going on. The Minister of Railways also stated in his address last night:
As a matter of fact, my hon. friend well knows, and the members from Prince Edward Island on this side of the house are in the best position to confirm it, that the question of a second car ferry for Prince Edward Island has been receiving the attention both of the Canadian National Railways and of the department for more than one year past.
That confirms the statement made by the Prime Minister in 1927. The Minister of Railways continued:
The members who sit on this side from the island have on several occasions waited upon myself, and have waited upon the management and officials of the Canadian National Railways, in connection with that matter, and were always given to understand that determination with respect to the matter would be reached by the government before the supplementary estimates were presented to the house.
That is a true statement. I happen to be a member of the select committee on railways and shipping and I was practically told that this matter would be looked after in the supplementary estimates. Some of our friends opposite have done a lot of talking, especially the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley), who appears to take a peculiar interest in our province, for which we thank him, but while he was talking, the members from Prince Edward Island were working in the interests of the province, and as a result

we have received the announcement which was made by the Minister of Railways last night. Speaking in this house on February 6 last I said, among other things:
So far as communication is concerned I believe that the government will carry into effect the recommendation of the Duncan commission, and provide another car ferry. Three years ago on the floor of this house I advocated that this matter should be dealt with, and I understand that the government for some time, through the Department of Railways, has been gatheriiig information and making preparations for this desired improvement. We are sincerely hopeful that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will see fit to place, if not in the main estimates at least in the supplementary ones, an appropriation for this much needed work.
The hon. member for Pictou in his address yesterday referred to the members from our province as rubber stamps. It is rather significant that although he might have been called to order for so doing, knowing the hon. gentleman as we do, nobody thought it worth while to call him to order. No member is supposed to be referred to in this house by another member as a rubber stamp. I think the remark was not in very good taste.

Would the hon. member
be good enough to repeat his statement in regard to rubber stamps? Does he say that I said the members from Prince Edward Island were rubber stamps?

Here is what the hon.
member said, at page 3258 of Hansard:
The members for Prince Edward Island on the government side are referred to as "rubber stamps."

Yes, referred to as that
in the paper from which I quoted.
It is immaterial anyway.

I was quoting from a
paper in the hon. member's own island and they should know.

The fact is that while the hon. gentleman has been talking, we have been working in the interests of the province, and we are very pleased to have this announcement which the Minister of Railways made last night. I again thank the minister and the government for promising to provide this improved service, and I am sure that the government will in future do anything it can to further the interests of Prince Edward Island.
Many members opposite are always talking of hard times. We do not agree with them in their doleful tales, because in our province things are prosperous and this action on the part of the government should be an occasion of further satisfaction to our people.

Steel Industry-Mr. Young (Weyburn)

I shall not detain the house many minutes, but I should like to set forth the views of another section of the country towards this resolution.
The resolution, as I understand it, asks for two things, bounties and increased tariffs. A bounty is asked for on coal, and I understand that the argument which is advanced in support of that request is that the steel companies in central Canada import their coal from the United States and have to pay a duty on it, but that when the coal is used for metallurgical purposes, they get a rebate of 99 per cent of the duty. The British Empire Steel Corporation, located in the maritime provinces, uses coal from its own mines, and therefore does not get any rebate because it does not pay any duty; it imports no coal. It therefore asks that the government give it a bounty, for using its own coal, which will be equal to the drawback received by the Steel Company of Canada on the duty it pays on the coal it imports from the United States. Every year since I have been in this house the people of the maritimes have been telling us that they could not sell their coal; people would not buy it; and they wanted the government to do something to help them find a market. Now they tell us they are not willing to burn their own coal unless we pay them a bounty. What would hon. gentlemen opposite think if the farmers of this country came to parliament and said: We want a bonus on every bushel of our own oats that we feed to our own horses? They would say it was a preposterous request. But not one bit more preposterous than the very request those men are making for a bounty on their own coal.
What is the need of the iron and steel industry in Canada? Is that industry in such a serious position as hon. gentlemen opposite would have us believe? I say it is not. The iron and steel industry of Nova Scotia, as I understand it, is devoted largely to the production of what are known as the primary iron and steel products, such as pigs, ingots, blooms and billets. Let us look at the value of the imports in those particular branches of the industry to-day as compared with what they were in 1922 when my hon. friends opposite were in power. We find that in 1922 the imports of pigs, ingots, blooms and billets amounted to $932,370; our exports of these commodities for the same year amounted to $622,919. In other words, our imports that year were 50 per cent greater than our exports. That condition continued until 1925. Then in 1926 the condition was reversed, and our imports in those forms of iron and steel amounted to $1,568,112; our exports,$2,167,172.
In the next year, 1927, we imported of the same forms $1,634,048, and exported $3,427,779. That is, our imports, which in 1922 were 50 per cent greater than our exports, in 1927 were only half as much as our exports. Our imports had increased by $700,000; our exports by four times that amount. Most of these imports, I understand, come from the United States.
It would be interesting to know whaJt was the situation in 1913, when the party of "No track or trade with the Yankees" was in power. In that year we imported pigs, ingots, blooms and billets to the value of $5.545;770; in 1927 we imported those forms to the value of $1,126,354. To that we have to add $507,783, imports of chrome steel, ferro silicon, and so on, making a total importation for 1927 of $1,634,127, as against $5,545,770 in 1913. If you make allowance for the difference in the value of the dollar in those two years, you will find the imports today about 15 per cent of what they were in those days.
These forms of iron and steel are the raw material of a great number of our other manufactures. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) pointed out the other day, some 300 manufacturers of other commodities depend on these forms for their raw material. What is the production, then, of the other forms of which these products are the raw material? We find that of castings and forgings, hardware and hooks, agricultural implements, machinery, automobiles, and so on, we manufactured in 1922 to the value of $187,137,608, and in 1926 to the value of $296,161.940- an increase of over $100,000,000. In 1922 we employed in these industries 40,700 men; in 1928, 57,050. I want to ask my hon. friends opposite: If we adopted the policy which they advocate and increased the duty on these forms of iron and steel, and therefore increased the cost of the raw material of these other industries, what would be the effect? We would jeopardize these other industries employing 57,000 men for the sake of the industry that is producing the raw material. Would we increase our market by that means? Now, what is the condition of the three great iron and steel companies in Canada; are they in as distressful circumstances as some people would have us believe? Let us look first at Besco. How about the Steel Company

Those are the companies, Mr. Speaker, who are now telling us that they are in such, dire straits and cannot survive unless the government lend them some assistance. It has been frequently stated that this government has discriminated against the primary iron and steel industry, and has favoured other industries at its expense. Let us compare the situation in the iron and steel industry with the situation in all manufacturing industries throughout the country. We find that in 1922 the iron and steel industry employed 75,354 men, paying them in wages, $91,629,491; and in 1926 they employed 103,510 men at a total wage of $137,640,065. All manufacturing industries in Canada in 1922 employed 387,689 men; in 1926, 499,733. The wages and

salaries paid were, in 1922 $497,113,554, and in 1926, $653,850,433. Comparing the figures then and now, we find that since 1922 the number of employees engaged in the steel industry has increased 34 per cent, and the wages 41 per cent ; while in all manufacturing industries the number of employees has increased 29 iper cent, and the wages 31 per cent. So we find that the number of employees in the iron and steel industry has increased more than the average in 'Canada, and the rate of wages has increased more than in the other industries.
Taking all these things into account, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the claim of the iron and steel industry for further consideration has absolutely no basis in faot, and is utterly unjustifiable.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Young) who has just taken his seat on the valuable statistics in connection with the steel industry which he has given to the house and to the country. It is amusing to notice that our hon. friends opposite are so anxious now to dispose of the debate and do not appear to wish any further discussion on their own amendment. It seems that the important announcement made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) last evening has rather taken the wind out of their sails, and now they are anxious to have their amendment disposed of as quickly as possible. However, before leaving the question, I desire to extend to the Minister of Railways, for the announcement he made last evening, the thanks of the people of my county, of all shades of politics. I think I am justified in making this statement, that the Liberal members on this side of the house could have given this information out some time ago. They had the assurance from the railway management and also from the minister that this important matter would be dealt with, but it was not our place to divulge any information that had been given us in confidence until the minister had seen fit to make an announcement in the house at the proper time.
The placing of a second car ferry on the route is something that benefits not only the province of Prince Edward Island but the whole of the maritimes and, in fact, the Dominion at large. Our province is not very considerable in area but we have a large trade. We buy largely from the manufacturers of the upper provinces and, in return, we ship out large quantities of produce; so that the car ferry, as I say, is of advantage not only to Prince Edward Island but to the

Steel Industry-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
whole Dominion, for it links up that province with the mainland and other parts of Canada.
In mj' opinion the very excellent speech made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has so cleared the situation as to render it unnecessary for me to go into details to show the way in which the Duncan report has been implemented. That report has 'been acted upon as well as it was humanly possible for any government to have acted upon a report in the time that has elapsed since it was brought down. Our friends opposite are demanding that the report be implemented 100 per cent. Now, hon. members on this side of the house, who were in the house when the commission was proposed, and when the government attempted to appoint that commission, will recollect how hon. gentlemen opposite objected. They objected to the appointment of a commission, declaring that it was only a means of sidestepping the issue. They said that the government would appoint the commission and that when that commission's report was submitted it would be laid away in the archives and never be implemented. They opposed to the hilt the appointment of the Duncan commission. But the commission was appointed and, after it had completed its labours it brought in a very comprehensive report dealing with every phase of the maritime situation. That report has been implemented almost 100 per cent. Anyone who reads the speech of the Minister of National Defence, and observes how carefully he took up question afer question mentioned in the report, will agree that the report has been fully implemented.
The 20 per cent reduction in freight rates represents to the people of the maritime provinces a boon which one can hardly estimate; we do not realize the amount of money it will mean. In their estimates the other day the government had the sum of $3,395,000 voted this year to make up to the Canadian National Railways the reduction in freights on that division. This is practical assistance not only to the shippers but to every industry in the maritimes; it extends an advantage to farmers, fishermen, manufacturers and merchants; it takes in everyone. In addition to that, the further reduction made on coal, in the way of subventions, which has been fully brought out by the Minister of National Defence, goes to show that in that respect alone the government has gone further than the recommendations made in the Duncan report.
Now I come to the subsidy. It would not be surprising if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) almost refused to pay that subsidy, after the manner in which our hon. friends
opposite have criticized the Finance department with regard to the method of paying the subsidy. It is really unfair that such criticism should be indulged in. There have been handed out these sums to the maritime provinces: Nova Scotia, $875,000; New Brunswick, $600,000; Prince Edward Island, $125,000. Under the circumstances, these payments being made at regular intervals along with the other subsidies, why in the world do our friends complain? They remind me of the clergyman who took as his text the reference to the devil who went about like a roaring lion seeking whom he might devour. The clergyman divided his subject under three heads: first, who the devil was he? secondly, where in the devil was he going? and thirdly, what in the devil was he roaring about? Our hon. friends opposite were roaring about something yesterday, when they were loud in their condemnations of the government. To-day they have not a word to say regarding the matter.
The Minister of Finance has treated us fairly, and the whole question is subject to further examination. It is to be looked into carefully, and if further subsidies are due the maritimes, I feel that we shall be dealt with fairly and that the grant will be increased. But I do not think that the way to secure that increase is by continually criticizing the government for the manner in which they have so far dealt with the Duncan report.
With regard to railway facilities and the improvements that have been made, one has only to look at the port development that has taken place in the province of Prince Edward Island, at Charlottetown, Summerside and Georgetown, to see what splendid advantages have been afforded. But as the Minister of National Defence has pointed out, over $5,000,000 has been voted between Halifax and St. John for port development. In view of this, I submit that our friends opposite should not be unreasonable enough to ask for anything further along these lines. I was pleased to note that the Minister of Railways last night stated that $40,000 would be allotted this year for additional terminal facilities at Summerside. This shows that the Canadian National system is improving its lines, when there is a demand for these facilities.
In the province of Prince Edward Island our trade has increased by leaps and bounds. As I pointed out before, railway stations that were to be closed, because they could not come up to the required amount of earnings, have improved to such an extent that whereas stations that were earning $10,000 three years

ago are now earning S50,000. I noticed in an item in the maritime press the other day that twenty-one new sidings had been asked for in the maritimes from the Canadian National Railways. It was evidence of progress when they required these additional facilities.
As a result of the survey carried out over the railway lines in the province of Prince Edward Island we hope that further improvements will be effected when the recommendations of this survey are turned in to the government. He has had experience over a number of years and is thoroughly familiar with the route and its requirements. He knows how docks should be built; he knows what arrangements should be made whereby automobiles may be placed on the car ferry under their own power instead of being loaded on flat cars as is the case at present, and I believe no one can give better advice in this matter.
Again I wish to thank the Minister of Railways for the important announcement which he has made; I hope a contract for this ship will be let soon and that we will have it in time to assist in moving the 1929 traffic.

It was not my intention to make any remarks in connection with this discussion; hon. members on this side have gone pretty well into the case as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, but in his remarks this afternoon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) would lead us to believe that the government had implemented the recommendations of the Duncan commission in connection with the fisheries of the maritime provinces. through the appointment of a deputy minister, and when the Prime Minister spoke in connection with the Duncan report last year he stated that a deputy minister would be appointed. I understood from my hon. friend that the government had carried out that recommendation by appointing that commission, which has just made its report. As I have said, it is not necessary for me to make any further remarks in connection with this matter because our case has been well put by the members who spoke last night. Our friends opposite are complaining because we have nothing further to say in the matter; I think we have said quite enough, and it will take the government some time to answer the case we have put forward.

This greatly reminds me of an accused person charged with theft on twelve counts. He is acquitted on eleven of the charges and the defence for the twelfth is that, having been acquitted on eleven, he should be acquitted on the twelfth. Or take it the other way; he is found guilty on eleven counts, and it is argued that having been found guilty on eleven counts he should be found guilty on the twelfth. After the whole of yesterday afternoon had been taken up in discussing among others the question of a car ferry between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, I was amazed to hear the Minister of Railways say that the government had placed a provision of a million dollars for this car ferry in the supplementary estimates. Then this afternoon I heard one of the hon. members from Prince Edward Island saying that it was not their place to disclose what was given in confidence.
The British North America Act provides that any moneys expended by this parliament shall carry with them the recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General, and that the estimates shall reach this house in certain well defined ways. For the first time in my limited experience, and I think in the experience of the oldest member of this house, a responsible minis teg of the crown rose in his place and told the house that a million dollars has been placed in the supplementary estimates for a given work. It is true that the question was asked whether it would be done or not, but the correct answer was that the matter was under consideration. Instead of that, the minister of the crown discloses what is to bo in the supplementary estimates. When he was reminded of the fact that the oath of a cabinet minister should prevent the disclosure of what takes place in council, he said he had the permission of the government to make that statement. That makes it even worse, because the oath of office of a privy councillor- I have taken the trouble to look it up-ia very clear upon that point. He swears:

oil, without publishing or disclosing the same or any part thereof, by word, writing, or any otherwise to any person out of the same council, but to such only as be of the council.

In connection with the Petersen investigation I recall that it was successfully urged that even the names of the men who appeared in council should not be given out. When you ask questions regarding policies that are under consideration by His Majesty's Privy Council for the Dominion, it is improper to disclose them, because it is a violation, when it involves the expenditure of money, of the British North America Act itself and of the oath of a privy councillor. more than $2,000,000 for the month of April. Is that not a good reason why this recommendation of Sir Andrew Duncan should be carried out? What did he tell us about this tariff advisory board? He told us that he preferred to trust his own common sense in other matters, and the house agreed with him, for thus far on any matter submitted to the board no findings of fact had been made which would enable the government to arrive at a conclusion. He has told us that this matter was before the tariff advisory board. Sir Andrew Duncan has also said that it was before the board. But nothing was done, nothing has been done, nothing is being done, and this country is faced with the fact that unless something is done, the reaction that is now setting in in the United States will be followed by depression in this country, such as has always followed depression in the United States. But if we now take the action that we are capable of taking in Canada, if we call up all our reserves, if we face the situation as we should, if we deal with conditions as Sir Andrew Duncan pointed out we should, we will develop our iron and steel industry in Cape Breton and be able to meet the situation, instead of buying increased quantifies of goods from the United States in the shape of iron and steel.
Remember this, that the steel question was the first matter submitted to this tariff advisory board, and it has not yet been dealt with. The minister himself has afforded to us the best reason why he should not rely upon that board. Any hon. member who followed the discussion with respect to the tariff advisory board when the textile schedules were before this house realizes that the Minister of Finance was more willing to trust his own common sense in dealing with those matters than the meanderings of this tariff board, which dealt with everything and found nothing, which laboured all night and produced nothing, like the fishermen upon the lake; they caught nothing, and this tariff board found nothing.

The economic condition of the American continent being what it is, we would be derelict in our duty, we would be faithless representatives of the people, if we did not point out that condition and ask this house to take the measures which Sir Andrew Duncan said should be taken, and taken promptly, mark you, with respect to this industry in order to save it from disaster.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the reason we make this motion on going into supply. The Minister of Finance was finding fault about the loss of time. It may be a loss of time, but in order that Canada may be able to face the conditions which will be upon us within a reasonable time unless all signs fail, unless the business barometers cannot be read as they should. Unless the predictions made by great business executives of the United States are not worthy of consideration, We should take steps first of all to curtail our expenditures and see to it that not a single dollar of the public money is spent unless it is productive; in other words, unless it will pay the interest upon the expenditure made. That is the first consideration.
Secondly, we should see to it that such legislation is placed upon the statute books of this country so that when the storm breaks and economic disaster or difficulty or setbacks threaten our nearby neighbours, we shall be fortified and strengthened to meet the storm without in any sense having disaster upon us. 
That is the reason I venture to urge this matter upon this house at this time. It is not a matter of whether you shall have a wharf here or a ferry there or a narrow-gauge railway yonder; these are insignificant administrative acts with respect to the Duncan report. The great problem is the development of the raw materials that Providence has given to us, the opening up of our great resources, the providing of employment for our people, the making of greater opportunities for our people in Canada. That is what the Duncan report dealt with, in order that the maritime provinces might become what they were intended to be-not that somebody might have a dollar spent here and somebody else have a dollar spent there, not that $50,000 should be spent for a wharf here or a bridge there. That is not what Sir Andrew, Duncan was talking about, but large problems of constructive statesmanship, and there is no larger problem of constructive statesmanship than the development of the iron and steel industry of this country, whether it be at the Soo, in Cape Breton, or at Hamilton. It is essential that that industry should be developed because under modem economic conditions steel is the life blood in the development of a country. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we urge upon this house that action should be taken, not next year, but this year, to remedy this grievance, and that the report made by the Duncan commission should be implemented and prompt action taken, not in 1929, but in 1928, while there is still time before the economic storm bursts upon this country.

I do not rise to take exception to this item; in fact I thoroughly approve of

it, and I hope that while I am a member of the house I shall have the opportunity of voting for a very much more substantial sum to complete this work. The purpose of the undertaking is to connect the Georgian bay with lake Ontario, using the various waterways and lakes which are to be found in the interior of Ontario between these points. The total length of the canal when completed will be 240 miles, but so extensive are the lakes and rivers which can be utilized that there will be only thirty-five miles of actual canal in the system when it is completed.
This work has been under consideration for a very long time. It is just one hundred years since the advantage of building the canal commended itself to the government of the day, and steps were taken to survey the system. The work was not immediately undertaken, but later on certain locks were built linking up a portion of the system. Then there was a long wait and finally, forty-two years ago, the work was again taken into consideration, and progress has been slowly made. The system is practically complete now except for a small portion of development required on the Severn river, and it would have been completed but for the intervention of the war.
The canal links up several important municipalities, such as Trenton, Campbellton, Lindsay, Orillia, Barrie and numerous other places. The lake system is a very extensive one. Lake Simcoe, of course, is very well known. The next largest lake is Rice lake, twenty miles in length and from two to three miles wide. Then there is Balsam lake, Stoney lake and others: and hundreds of other lakes find an outlet into the canal system. The district has become a very attractive one for tourists, and all along the canal system you will find summer cottages and hotels. If the canal were completed I think it would be a still more attractive place to the tourists. We cannot overlook this trade; it brings millions and millions of dollars annually into this country, and it should be encouraged. I understand that the minister is contemplating a visit to the system. I extend' to him my endorsement of the invitation which has already been given him, and I am quite sure that after he has spent two or three days examining the system he will consider favourably the final construction of the Trent canal.

was there before the canal was built. However that may be, the Dominion, rightly or wrongly, agreed to pay forty per cent of $100,000, and the Dominion kept that agreement to the letter. The counties concerned in building the bridge did not, as I say, accept the lowest tender. Whether that was the reason why the cost overran $100,000, I am not in a position to say. The fact remains that the cost exceeded $100,000, but the Dominion fulfilled every obligation it ever assumed in connection with the Atherley bridge. The question now is: Should the Dominion be even more generous and share in the expenditure over and above the $100,000? The matter has been before the treasury board on more than one occasion and the treasury board has not seen fit at any time to recognize the claim. I regret that I cannot say anything more favourable than that to my hon. friends.

May I correct the minister? I do not know for the life of me how he can say that the Dominion has no obligation in the matter. The extra expenditure was incurred owing to the fact that they had to have a swing bridge or the canal would have been blocked. The counties did

not need a swing bridge; the swing bridge was built for the purpose of navigation only and it does go over part of the canal. It is the part connecting the two lakes. After the agreement was entered into the department insisted upon some changes which helped to run up the expense. For instance they had to have an electrical apparatus installed to turn the bridge in one minute instead of having it turned by hand. That accounts for part of the extra expense. Surely the minister cannot deny that the government is responsible for part of the extra expenditure, because if that swing bridge had not been built there, the canal would have been useless; it would have been blocked. I cannot see the force of the minister's argument.

The point that seems to
confuse both the minister and the counties is whether there was an absolute statement on either side that the costs were to be held down to $100,000 and that the government were obligated to pay only forty per cent of that amount. I submit that the letter which was written by the department distinctly gave the counties to understand that the government would pay forty per cent of the total cost.
. Mr. DUNNING: I should like to see such a letter, because if any undertaking was given by any government to pay more than the $40,000, I would consider it my duty to recommend that that obligation, entered into in that manner, be implemented. If he can produce an authentic or official document from this or any other government committing the government to more than has already been paid, 1 shall be glad to have the matter considered again in the light of that undertaking.

I do not think anybody
could expect any government or any person to take a sounder stand than the minister has taken, and I would humbly request him to ask the department to show him the letter which was written and which is in its possession, that misled the counties.

My officials inform me,

I should not like to say that such a promise was made definitely in the contract. I submit that there is a letter on file. It was read in my presence. I will have that further looked into.

When the agreement was entered into, the county was to pay 60 per cent and the government 40 per cent, but later the government insisted that a swing bridge should be built. That increased the cost, and I think it is only reasonable that the government should bear its share of this increased cost.

My hon. friend forgets that the stream in question is a navigable stream. At that point it is not canalized, and regardless of whether or not the canal had been built, the counties could not build a bridge which would obstruct that stream. They would have to make provision for the navigation of the stream, and they did. The fact that a swing bridge was put in has nothing whatever to do with the building of the canal further along the same watercourse. On no navigable stream may a bridge be built which has the effect of obstructing navigation. The argument that the swing bridge was put in because of the Department of Railways and Canals is entirely erroneous. So far as the swing portion of the bridge is concerned, I am advised that the department looks after its maintenance, and also pays the cost of keeping a man to operate it. On the whole, I must say that iby comparison with similar matters elsewhere, I do think these counties were very generously treated by the particular government and minister who entered into that agreement in the first place. But if there is any commitment by this government, by a minister, or by an official who was authorized to enter into such an arrangement at the time, or anything of the kind, I shall be very glad to have it looked into again. I am not speaking of any promises which may
have been made since the bridge was built; that is another matter entirely. But with respect to the arrangement which resulted in the building of the bridge, if there is anything of the sort in existence we will have the whole matter reconsidered.
Is it not a fact that the changes were made at t'he instance of the government after the agreement was completed, changes which increased the cost?

My officers inform me that the plans weTe submitted in the usual way, but as the bridge was being built certain defects were found owing to the nature of the ground underneath the piling, and it was insisted that stronger piling should be used in connection with the centre portion of the bridge; otherwise, the bridge would not have stood.

That would increase the cost to that extent. That was done after the agreement was made. I am also credibly informed, and I believe it is a fact, that the government demanded other expenditures, for instance, on electrical machinery, instead of hand power for turning the bridge. That also was done after the agreement was made, and it considerably increased the cost. As the government insisted on that being done, I think it should pay the whole of that extra expenditure.
That was part of the original agreement.

I am told not. It was long after the original agreement was confirmed, and for the life of me I cannot see how the government can get away from bearing its fair share of this increased cost. It is true that the ground proved to be rather unsuitable for the foundations, and that increased the cost. The government, according to the original agreement, bear 40 per cent of the cost and the counties 60 per cent, and I think any additional expenditure should be borne in the same proportion. These unforeseen expenditures cannot be looked after at the time the bargain is made, and since part of this increased cost is due to the demands made by the government, and the government's demand increased the cost tenfold, I think the government should at least bear its share of this extra cost.

there, the whole Niagara district has become industrialized, especially between Niagara Falls, Welland, Port Colborne and the village of Port Dalhousie. I urge the minister to do something definite under this item. The question that occurs to me is this: What is going to become of the existing canal in 1930 when the government opens the new Welland ship canal? Active measures should be taken this summer to get rid of the congestion which exists at the present time on this existing canal. That canal will be utilized next summer almost every moment of the night and day and I trust that in the coming summer additional money will be forthcoming for further dredging at the lake Ontario end of the canal at Port Dalhousie and at Port Arthur and on the central section. It is important to know what action will be taken in regard to the lake levels. I do not know what the reason is, but the levels have gone down and there are many complaints in this regard from Thorold, St. Catharines and other places of shallow water in this channel. diversion I do not know, but I do know that there has been a good deal of complaint regarding the levels there. I hope the minister will spare no effort, in view of the heavy tonnage passing through the canal, to get rid of the congestion which to-day is hampering the movement of vessels. Action should be taken at the earliest possible moment to cope with the very heavy tonnage that is sure to go up this year. The government can well afford to be liberal and keep the work going on repairs and renovations at this busy canal all summer and also hasten as much as possible the completion of the new Welland ship channel, as it will not be completed one day too soon to cope with the huge volume of tonnage congesting the present canal all the time by night and by day.

The committee ought to have some information bearing on the operation of the canal, in view of the remarks of my hon. friend1; because I am bound to say, after paying the matter of Welland some rather close personal attention last year, the whole Welland operation-both the operation of the existing canal and the construction of the new canal-reflects very great credit indeed upon the Canadian engineering profession. That can be best illustrated in relation to the existing canal when I point out that there was a considerable increase of tonnage passing through the present canal in the calendar year 1927. In 1926 there passed through 5,214,000 tons of cargo and in 1927, 7,247,000 tons, or an increase of over 2,000,000 tons in one year of cargo passing through the existing canal. When one takes into account the fact that the operation of the existing canal is hampered very considerably by immense construction works going on in some places, crossing the existing canal, and that it is necessary to pass ships through the existing canal while at the same time constructing new works, one can appreciate the nature of the work that is being done. Engineers who have come from other countries in the past year have expressed in the very highest terms their opinion of the engineering importance of the great work which is being accomplished in the construction of the new Welland ship canal-with which I shall deal under another vote-by the Canadian engineers. By way of illustration of the volume of business, I would point out to those members from the west, who know something about the handling of grain through elevators, that the 3,000,000 bushel elevator operated by the Department of Railways and Canals at

Port Colborne handled last year 77,600,000 bushels of grain. That was the extent of its operations during the last calendar year. I do not think there is a piece of grain-handling machinery in the Dominion that can show a record superior to that-a complete turnover, twenty-six times, in the handling of this grain. The previous year the amount handled was 62,535,000 bushels as compared with 77,621,000 in the last calendar year, with a capacity, as I have indicated, of approximately 3,000,000 bushels of storage. Of course, it is a transfer house; but these figures will give an indication of the importance of this artery.
With reference to my hon. friend's question as to what we shall do with the existing canal when the new canal is completed, I may point out to the committee that there have been four Welland canals, including the new one. Parts of three of them are still in existence, and it is somewhat of a problem to work out to the best advantage the utilization of the channels, the water, and so on, of the former canals. As an engineering matter it has not yet been fully worked out what we shall do with the present canal when the new one is completed.
But all the water will be diverted finally through the new canal.

There are qualifications
even to that; from Thorold to Dalhousie that is the case. However, these problems are being looked into continuously by our engineering staff, and the fact that we have not yet reached a conclusion as to exactly what shall be done in connection with a matter of such magnitude does not indicate dilatoriness on the part of those responsible. I assure the committee that due care and consideration will be given the problem.
