I do not wish to go into the details of this item but I do desire to protect against the very heavy increases which are manifest in the national defence estimates this year. I presume that some of the papers will say I am making my annual protest, but I am very glad to be able still to protest againfet these expenditures, and there is. a very real reason for protest this year since in the last two years the estimates for this department have increased almost fifty per cent.
Last year the minister rather resented my references to professional militarists; he said

Supply-National Defence
he had yet to meet a professional militarist. I should like to say that when we speak about professional militarists and their influence we simply mean what we mean when we speak of other professional men; we refer to a man who is a professional soldier, whether he is a private or an officer. I think possibly the minister himself is a splendid example of a man whose job it is to magnify alnd efficiently run his department. I have every admiration for a man who wishes to make a success of what he undertakes; I think we would not admire a minister if he did anything else, but since there are men whose job it is to make a success of military things; since there are officers who very naturally, from their viewpoint, are trying to make their military establishment efficient, we who are opposed to military expenditure can quite rightly suggest that undoubtedly their continual effort is to increase expenditures, just as is the aim of officials in other departments.
Last year the minister stated:
I am presiding over the Department of National Defence, not over a department which has to do with the propagation of the principle of abolition of war.
I think that is a clear-cut statement; in fact I am inclined to think it a little nearer the truth than the statement he made during another debate in this house, when he described himself as the minister of peace. I wish he were the minister of peace; in that case I would be very glad to entrust to him a good deal of money in order to create an effective peace department. But let me repeat what he said last year:
. I am presiding over the Department of National Defence, not over a department which has to do with the propagation of the principle of abolition of war.
So he is very clearly at the head of that department, trying to make it effective from his standpoint. He went on to say that he proposed:

to see that we have at least some form of defence such as that which is regarded as necessary, having regard to conditions in the world.
In this connection I noticed a very good statement in the Toronto Daily Star, to this effect:
So far all attempts to disarm even partially have been doomed to failure because the international representatives who meet to discuss the problem have been admirals and generals professionally interested in improving the world's war preparedness, and incapable of believing that the whole thing ought to be, or could be, ended.
That is the point I should like to make, and in this view I think I am sustained by
no less an authority than Lloyd George, who *in one of his recent letters made the fallowing statement:
In every country, it is a part of the business of the fighting staff to work out plans for defence against all conceivable enemies. Their minds get absorbed in these brilliant schemes. They gloat over their efficiency, and like every inventor, yearn to put their machine to a test. In the secrecy of their department, the possible war soon becomes a likely war, and the likely gradually glides into the inevitable war. It is at first discussed in whispers behind locked doors. Then at clubs where gather together men whose patriotism is above any suspicion of being tempered by discretion. .	. The next
stage is always the after dinner speech.
Then, as he says, comes the surrender to fools. William Leach, when Under Secretary for the air ministry for England, suggested that if peace were wanted peace must be prepared for. Let me give a comment on this from the Manitoba Free Press:
Naturally such a revolutionary proposal-
Such as was made by Mr. Leach at that time.
-namely, reliance upon Christianity to attain peace, provoke a storm of protest. Major General J. E. B. Seely, Liberal member of parliament, and Rear Admiral N. F. Sueter, Conservative, were among Mr. Leach's opponents in the debate, the former exclaiming: "If the empire is to be defended by Sermons on the Mount, God help them."
The Free Press goes on:
It is easy to picture the righteous indignation of choleric political colonels, retired admirals and many others who pride themselves upon being practical men, living in a practical world. In spite of the ghastly failure of the policy of just such very practical persons in 1914, they are back to the same old cry of preparedness for the next war to ensure peace.
The minister does not like quotations. I gave him some last year, and I give these tonight simply because while a good many people may not particularly care what I say with regard to these things, they cannot altogether dlisregard the opinions of men who stand high in the councils of the nation, some of whom even stand high in military matters. Let me quote an authority whom I think the minister will recognize. Sir William Robertson, speaking before the chamber of commerce at Lincoln, England, said:
We no longer agree that the best way to prevent war is to prepare for it. Instead of preventing war, we know that preparations are likely to precipitate it.
So I ask the reason for the development of militarism in Canada-because let us make no mistake; there is a steady increase in our military expenditures, and these expenditures are a very fair indication as to where our interests and our policies really lie. I happened to be in Montreal only last Sunday;

Supply-National Defence

there I watched a long parade which took almost an hour to pass. The newspapers said there were nearly 10,000 people in that parade. The salute was given to the Minister of National Defence, and we almost seemed to be back in the days from 1914 to 1918. It is quite true there were only a few veterans in that parade, but unfortunately we had a great many young chaps and even young boys parading. I cannot but think that this kind of thing is encouraging the military spirit. Why are we seeking to develop that spirit in Canada? I cannot but recall some words of Dr. E. J. Dillon in The Inside Story of the Peace Conference, as follows:
Imperialism and militarism are striking roots in soil where they were hitherto unknown. In a word Prussianism instead of being destroyed has been openly adopted by its ostensible enemies.
It is all very well to say that our militarism in Canada is very different from Prussian militarism. I am firmly convinced that militarism is very much the same the world over, whether in Germany, Great Britain, France, Japan, or in Canada, for that matter, although I am thankful to think that so far we have not progressed as far as some of the older nations. But we are on the way, unless there is some very definite check given to present tendencies.
In the old days in which many of us grew up in Canada we did not have these military ideals to the extent we have to-day. We did not have the military spirit that has been fostered in the last few years, and we did not have these very heavy expenditures for war. Immediately after the war we said that we had learned our lesson-that the world had learned a lesson-and we were proceeding to try something better. It would seem that even though we talk peace, even though we are a member of the League of Nations and are talking these days of arbitration treaties, we in Canada are still pursuing this military idea.
We all want peace; the minister agrees with that. But the minister and his department, and a considerable number of people in Canada, believe that peace can be secured by military armaments and by defence. They are sincere; I grant them that. They consider themselves patriotic. But those of us who differ are also sincere, and we believe that their policy will lead this country to ruin. We have the right, I would say the duty, to defeat that policy.
The Minister of Finance has made the statement that half our natural revenue goes to pay the interest on the debt incurred in the last war. In spite of the futility of that
TMr. Woodsworth.]
war-its failure to settle any of the grave economic or international questions, we are preparing to assume our share in some next war that will not be very long in coming if other nations adopt the policies that we are adopting. In every other estimate that comes before this house we ask the purpose of the expenditure. I think we should be distinctly told, in connection with these estimates, against whom we are preparing to fight. Some of the militarists accuse us of being dreamers and impossible idealists. I accuse them of being romantic sentimentalists, and I would say to them, against whom are we in Canada preparing to fight?
Anyone that attacks us.

Anyone that attacks us! We are making our preparations to-day and we are looking around for potential enemies who are likely to do the attacking. Can you imagine that we are going to be drawn into another great European war? I can hardly think that when I talk with the men who returned from the last war. I had a letter the other day from a returned veteran of the war, and in speaking of his own boy he said, "I will never let him go to war. I have done my bit for the both of us, and before he goes I would do something desperate." That is the opinion of not a few of the returned men.

Very few.

and I know whereof I speak. I have spoken with hundreds, and I think into the thousands, who have expressed this view to me.
Are we going to war against the United States? If we are, let us come out frankly and say so. Are we preparing for war against the United States? In a recent book by Commander Ken worthy, entitled Peace and War, I noticed the following:
So strong a part does sentiment play in such matters that the great majority of Canadians would probably decide for immediate intervention on the side of the mother country.
That is in case of war between Great Britain and the United Staites. Then he goes on:
Yet this would mean a terrible war on Canadian soil. Automatically the Americans would invade Canada, and Britain, fighting in both the Pacific and the Atlantic, would forego other naval campaigns, including colonial raids and

trade attacks so as to permit the throwing of as many British troops and aeroplanes from ail parts of the empire on to Canadian soil in as short a time as possible. . . If Canada were invaded, a long-drawn-out and bloody land and aerial war would follow to add to the horrors of the naval campaigns.
Later on he says:
For the benefit of humanity and the good of the people concerned it would be better on the whole if Canada declared for neutrality. Such a declaration would limit the area of the struggle and make an earlier ending to it easier. And again he says:
But there is something greater than nationalist patriotism; and taking a long view, which is also a more humane view, it would be better for Canada to keep out.
When we have such advice from a Britisher of the standing of Commander Kenworthy, I think we might very well ask whether we are right in preparing for a possible war with the United States.
Are we preparing for war in the orient? Again, very few of us in Canada think that that is the way in which we can settle our problems on the Pacific. The most clearcut statement for armaments that I have seen from a Canadian source is that contained in a document published by the Navy League of Canada. It is entitled Interdependence of Canadian Industry and Naval Defence. He says that national security

-may some day lie in mutual treaties for ever lasting peace based on international economic adjustment; to-day unfortunately, it lies only in a proper measure of armed defence.
I think that is a fair statement of the case from the standpoint of the militarists. They talk of arbitration in order to wave it aside; they talk about treaties and say that treaties offer no security, and they come back again and again and say that the only way in which we can have world peace, the only way in which we can attain national security is by force of arms. It is that position that some of us challenge to-night. The document to which I have referred admits that the provision of armaments has not in the main prevented war, but warns that when a clash occurs, as it inevitably will under the existing economic system-
-stability of industrial commitments will lie only with those in a position to maintain their sea communications.
Again going back to the old and indefensible British position with regard to sea power.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Does he not think an examination of the territorial lines which resulted from the Versailles treaty would show that many other wars would be inevitable in consequence of that treaty?

That is a rather
large question into which I am not prepared to go to-night. It seems to me that the boundaries as drawn in Europe after the war were very arbitrary and in themselves are likely to provoke war in the future. I should like to see an early revision of the Versailles treaty. I am not, however, so sure that the drawing of new political boundaries will be the way to ensure peace. I think we shall have to go deeper than that and get at the underlying economic causes. In that connection I should like to quote one other sentence from this statement of the Navy League:
It is the everlasting economic war which prevails, in time of nominal peace, which has produced, and will produce, physical war.
There, it seems to me, is a clearcut statement, a frank recognition of the real cause of modem war, namely, the everlasting economic war which prevails in time of nominal peace. In view of such a situation, may we not ask whether there is no way out. Are we to go on forever exploring blind alleys? Are we to go on forever in the old ways that have proved absolutely futile in the settlement of these great economic problems; or have we not come to the time when we can tackle the big economic questions and attempt to discover some solution along other lines than those of the past?
I want to give one other quotation from the Manitoba Free Press which sets forth the position of a large number of Canadian citizens to-day:
It may take some time possibly several years, to get national animosities worked up to the due pitch for another war. But, in the economic conflict, the warfare for markets and concessions abroad, the activities of financial groups are more apparent than in the ten years or so leading up to the last war.
The pressure on the financial system has been intensified. The capacity of industrial nations to increase output has been enormously increased. The belief is commonly held in every country that wider markets must be found: the industries have to take care of increased overhead charges, due to recent industrial expansion, and industry everywhere is saddled with the burden of war debt.
As the system is operated at present, the only outlet according to orthodox financial belief is in exporting to markets abroad. But the markets abroad are being reduced, by reduced purchasing power, and themselves becoming industrialized. More nations than ever are looking for markets abroad, or preparing
Supply-N ational Defence

to cut into the business of competitive exporting The belief that it is vital to secure control of such an outlet as the untapped resources of Asia Minor is based on falsehood. It is one of the fallacies of orthodox finance. But it is leading to war, unless the lead is given by some nation towards a policy of increasing purchasing power at home-to open up the home market.
There we have a suggested solution of the great economic problem. Instead of making every effort to solve that economic problem, which is to-day not merely a national but a world problem, we are now turning back and attempting to prepare to fight those enemies with whom our present industrial and financial policy may bring us into conflict.
We who protest may be small in numbers, at least in this chamber, but I urge that in this matter we represent a very large section of the people of Canada. Canada has an opportunity for leadership in the campaign for peace. As I have said on previous occasions we are in a very unique position. As a member of the British Empire and as a member of the League of Nations we are linked up with the great majority of the nations of the world. On the other hand we live side by side with the great United States republic which is recognized as being a leading force in international finance. We are, a natural link, between these two great groups of powers. We are safe as regards invasion from the United States. No one to-day thinks that the United States are going to attempt a political invasion of Canada. There may be peaceful penetration by finance and industry, but we are safe from political invasion. Why cannot we take a bold step and lead the other nations along these lines of peace? To-day by permitting ourselves continually to increase our armaments, we are simply preparing the way for further trouble. You remember, Mr. Chairman, those lines of Israel Zangwill on "The God of War' .
"To safeguard peace, we must prepare for war"
I know that maxim; it was forged in hell.
This wealth of ships and guns inflames the vulgar	.
And makes the very war it guards against.
I have every respect for the way in which the minister is carrying out the work of his department; I can quite understand his ambitions to make that department effective; but I would urge upon the house that it is not the professional soldiers nor the Department of National Defence that ought to determine the extent to which we prepare for war in this country. That is a matter of

policy which ought to be decided by the house. More than that, if in some way the public at large could directly voice its attitude on this question, I have not the slightest doubt that the referendum would indicate opposition to the extension of military expenditures.

We are having once again the annual debate on peace and war. I may say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that the soldiers who fought for Canada were just as fond of peace as he is or anybody else who is preaching peace in this country to-day. Since I have been in the house these estimates have been cut down from $15,000,000 to $10,000,000 and to-day they are so cut to the bone that unless you want to cut the whole thing out altogether, you cannot cut another dollar off. The minister has been a very economic minister; he has held an even balance between the peace and the war party; he has gone over his department from coast to coast, and he has brought his estimates down to-night In answer to that all we hear is about war debts and authorities on peace. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does not require to quote any authorities on peace. He and the League of Nations are the most shining authorities on peace. He argues that we should cut the whole thing out and work for peace. The minister is working for peace on a preparedness basis. We have had enough Monroe doctrines and scraps of paper like the Washington conference and the Kellogg scrap of paper to be. We have the League of Nations which is the most troublesome institution in the world to-day. The only real League of Nations is the British fleet which in the last war protected our shores and protected us from slavery worse than anything in the history of the world. Had it not been for the British fleet in the late war we would have experienced the awful horrors of war on our own soil in Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg and Vancouver. As for what Canada does in a militia sense, as compared with the motherland and Australia and New Zealand, Canada gives in money a contribution of two pence halfpenny to militia and defence. The motherland pays the whole cost of a magnificent fleet to protect our Shore, to maintain our trade routes and to enable us to do business on the seven seas of the world, while we who in the darkest hours of the war were prepared to accept the protection of the British fleet and all the privileges we enjoyed as part of the British Empire should now be prepared to accept some of the responsibility which that incurs

and contribute adequately to maritime freedom. Yet we do nothing but sponge on the British taxpayer for our protection, and whine and complain about our mythical status.
Canada has failed as no other country in the late war has failed to give places in the armies of industry to Canadians who gave themselves places in the armies of liberty. Talk about peace and war! Let me tell the gentlemen of the Labour party that I do not believe that they are expressing the real views of the labour men of this country. The labour men, the trades unionists, of this country and the working classes enlisted as did no other class of the community. There were 50,000 of them who joined the colours and were killed, fighting for their country. Talk about the United States! Over 100,000 of the men who left for the front to fight this country's battles, when they came back here, could find no work to do, and they were driven out of Canada to the United States, by the economic policy of free trade which the hon. gentlemen of the Labour party advocate, to seek a living in the United States.
What do my hon. friends propose as a substitute for these estimates? The Monroe doctrine? Will that protect the shores of Canada? No. Will the new peace proposals of Mr. Kellogg protect this country? No, that, like the Monroe doctrine, will be another scrap of paper. It seems to me that every time they have an election on the other side of the line the Democratic or the Republican party spring a new league of nations or a peace pact or peace note of their own, and they put it over England and France and all the fellows who did the actual fighting, while they themselves were too proud to fight. They had a Washington conference in the days of President Harding, whereby Great Britain and France and the United States were to build no more capital ships for about forty years. Did the Americans keep that pact? No. Immediately after the war they turned all their war-time plants on the Atlantic ocean, at New York, New Haven and Savannah and other ports, into peacetime plants, and they started building a merchant navy by twenty-five and fifty and a hundred ships at a time, so that in a few years they will be equal to the British Empire in that respect. That is the way they kept the last pact. Did the Americans keep the Washington conference of five years ago? No. A bill was brought into the last congress, at the instance of President Coolidge, calling for a large expenditure for new capital ships for the navy and ships for the merchant marine and a huge navy vote, so much so that their
expenditure to-day is the largest of any nation in the world. Now that another election is coming on across the line, they put their heads together and evolve a new scrap of paper called the Kellogg plan, to end war until after the next presidential election when the jingoes will again be on top.
It is said now that we are a new nation. If we are a nation, we can declare war and are a sovereign power. The Kellogg note says we are or thinks so. The people of this country have never been asked to vote on this magnificent new status which we are supposed to have. It is a mere mockery, a sham, and a humbug all along to talk of our having a different status and being a nation. W e are not a nation. We are part of the British Empire to-day, and when Britain is at war Canada is at war. We are a link in a chain of free commonwealths within and making up the British Empire. We are not a free and independent nation. We are sponging to-day on the motherland for the cost of the protection of our Atlantic and Pacific coasts and our shipping on the seven seas. We contribute not a cent to the British fleet. We have a contemptible little navy of three or four stone hooker boats that hug the shore and are too proud to go out on the ocean and fight, and if they do go out on the ocean they have under the Laurier navy to send a wireless to Ottawa and have an order in council passed before they can fight when they see the enemy coming. I was on the Pacific last March at the time of the threatened war with China, and a Vancouver paper came out in a special edition headed "War is to be Declared," and asked what was going to protect the Pacific coast. The British Empire got out of its alliance with Japan, mainly owing to Canada's falling down.
The British Empire was also urged by Canada to drop its plans for a naval base at Singapore for the protection of our Pacific province, Australia and New Zealand in the event of another war. There will be wars as long as time lasts. You can talk about the mythical League of Nations, but I believe that there will be war as long as time lasts, and the country that prepares itself for war is doing more for peace than all the so-called peace agencies and talkfests on peace which I have heard in this house and out of it ever since I came into it.
Let me tell my hon. friends who are shouting from the house tops about peace that the half a million soldiers who fought for this country in France and Flanders are just as strong for peace, and ten times stronger, than those in this house and out of it who are shouting peace, because they went to the front
Supply-National Defence

and experienced the horrors of war. Canada lost fifty thousand men in the great war; many thousands more came back wounded and are now lying helpless in the hospitals, and some of them cannot get into the hospitals; some are starving and out of work because they are not one hundred per cent efficient, while we can spend nearly two millions on a farcical League of Nations. Many of these soldiers had to go to the United States to look for a living. The Canadians who joined the Canadian expeditionary force and served overseas from 1914 to 1918 have done more for peace than all those who stayed at home and are shouting peace from the house tops and served Canada better than Canadians on the voters' lists have served Canada in the polling booths from 1919 to 1926.
This League of Nations provides a fine Cook's tour for government officials and ministers. The League of Nations has provoked more strife than it has settled. It is the disturber of the peace of the British Empire, this so-called League of Nations to which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre is so fond of referring and similar mock debating societies on peace, and one day the British Empire will wake up and realize that they have been living in a fool's paradise as they were in 1909 if they listen much longer to the League of Nations and the peace party and the pacifists. We have spent $1,600,000 on the League of Nations, in joy rides and trips for officials and tourists. Talk about having a seat in the League of Nations; you might as well have a seat in the American baseball league or the National league. These leagues do more for peace with the Americans than the League of Nations. The League of Nations has done nothing for Canada and the empire but cause trouble and provide nice soft jobs and travelling expenses for officials and those who shout peace from the house tops in this country in season and out of season, while others who did the real work of protecting the people of this country, in the darkest hours of the war are driven in peace to the United States looking for a job and are exiled from Canada.
I am sorry that the minister has not included in his annual estimates a table showing the comparative contributions to defence that are made by the motherland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Our contribution amounts to about two shillings per head; in fact I do not think it is that much; I had the figures here, but unfortunately I have mislaid them. The figures for Australia and New Zealand are five or six times what ours are. They are paying for the Singapore base. We pay nothing. New Zealand, a

country with a population less than the city of Montreal, is contributing $5,000,000 over a period of years for the support of the Singapore base, and has contributed battleships to the British fleet. The Pacific question will be the great question before the people of this country to-morrow. I believe that the minister has pared his estimates down to the bone. You, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Power), know more about war than all the peace parties put together, because our gallant chairman as a young man sacrificed his position and went to the war, and I do not believe he will ever be the same man again. You, Mr. Chairman, have seen the errors made by the people of this country in the lack of preparations for war, and the cost of unpreparedness, and you know what it has cost the people of this country at Valcartier and in other parts of Canada in training as a result.
The cadet movement in this country is very largely paid for by the boards of education throughout Canada and the municipalities. Ontario will support the cadet movement as long as time lasts. That is the policy of the government at Queen's Park and through the municipalities they are spending a large amount of money on the cad'et movement. Those who are in the nonactive militia-I see my hon. friend from Parkdale in the house, but I did not see him in the war parade last Sunday. I know that in his Irish regiment and in many other units in Toronto the officers, the non-commissioned officers and men -have to dig down into their own pockets to provide part of the uniforms, equipment and stationery, and almost everything else for their units. That is what they have to do in the soldier city of Toronto. These are men now in the active militia at Toronto. They admire the present minister and the support he is giving them. He is holding the balance very evenly between the war party and the peace party in this country. The peace party are those who depend' on the Monroe doctrine, the League of Nations, the Kellogg note and similar scraps of paper to say nothing of the Washington note of five years ago. In my constituency in the Earls-court section there are twenty-four war widows in one block; they know something about war. Many of them have to go out to work, as a result of Canada's failure, and they are just as strong for peace as my hon. friend who has just spoken. Notwithstanding all this dream about our new status, notwithstanding the fact that last year we spent from $300,000 to $400,000 celebrating Dominion day, many of the returned men who fought the battles of -their country have had to go

to the United States to find jobs. Talk about what the United States is doing for peace! I know no country in the world that is doing more to prepare for war in their army and navy votes. Preparedness will do more to ensure peace than any other agency, as the late Lord Roberts pointed out years ago. The minister b&s not enough baoking; his estimates are not half large enough to put the militia on a proper basis. The item for spring camps is not half large enough. Only a few units are taken care of and the camps are small and not what they were. Many units cannot drill in camp; they have to drill in their home towns by night, as a result of such false economy.
Then we are spending nothing on maritime freedom; we are loading those bills off on the hard-pressed taxpayers of Great Britain. In the province of Ontario the population is mostly British born and they know something of what the mother country has done for maritime freedom. Certainly, had it not been for the British fleet, neither Canada nor the United States would have been able to send any troops overseas or send supplies or keep our trade routes open. There should be a day of reckoning for the peace party in this country. We can no longer continue to sponge on Great Britain for naval defence. Take the Pacific question; the teeming millions of China and Japan aTe within a few days of our western shores, and yet on the Pacific we have only one or two ships recently purchased. True, we have a few fishing and rowing boats, but so far as a fleet is concerned, we are not even a twenty-fifth class naval power.
I think these votes have been very carefully prepared and the only fault I have to find is that they have been cut down too low. But I shall support the minister. In the province of Ontario, which pays over 40 per cent of the cash taxes of Canada, 95 per cent of the people are in favour of these votes. I know something of the Trades Union movement in the city of Toronto. No movement in this country contributed more men to the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and they are the backbone of the militia, rank and file. I repeat, I shall support these votes, but they are not half enough. So far as they go, however, I think they will commend themselves to the wisdom and the judgment of the country generally.

Mr. Chairman, when
in 1925 I made my first speech against cadet training the total vote was about $11,000,000; this year it is $18,726,946.42. That is a very
large increase. This is done under a government which on every possible occasion protests that it is a peaceful government. We'll, looking over the treasury benches one would agree that at least it is a peaceful looking government. Yet these national defence votes have gone on increasing year after year. We used to have a Minister of National Defence who though he looked like a Prussian war lord, did not act like one; but to-day we have as minister of the department a gentleman who looks peaceful enough but acts like a Prussian war lord. Again, I entreat the Prime Minister to transfer his Minister of National Defence to a department where his great ability and driving force will be of greater benefit to Canada. Naturally the minister wishes to make a success of his department, but to the extent that he accomplishes this he makes hypocrites of Canadians, for all the time we are protesting that we are trying to promote the peace of the world as we listen to plans for peace made by leading Britishers and Americans and also by some of our own countrymen. And we have a place on the council of the League of Nations. It is a farce for us to send representatives to the League of Nations unless we back them up by peace sentiment in Canada. And if they are so backed up, why in the world do we not show that peace sentiment in the estimates? This fact is abundantly clear: Supposing preparedness does bring peace-and I do not think for a moment it does-under the new methods of carrying on war all the amounts of money we are voting for old methods are a straight waste. Training men to ride horses beautifully, dressing them up in blue and red coats, and putting on high class military parades such as the one put on last Sunday in Montreal, glorifying the whole spectacle and making it appear a grand thing-all this is just so much waste. We might as well use the money for some sensible purpose in Canada, because wars are no longer carried on in that fashion. Even since the last war a great deal of progress has been made. Only yesterday we all read in the newspapers of poisonous gas escaping accidentally from a tank in Germany, and finding its way, through open windows, into private houses, killing some people and destroying horses, cattle and vegetation everywhere. This is the new method. In the future wars will be carried on largely from the air, so that all this silly swank, this dressing up in pretty uniforms and parading on beautiful horses, will be absolutely useless. What will be the sense of a lot of men going around on horses, all dressed up, and thinking themselves fright-

fully big fellows? I say, it will be just so much waste of money. I do not. know how much this demonstration in Montreal cost the country, but no doubt it took a good deal of money. They had the cadets out and the minister of peace was present to inspect the whole affair. They simply glorified the whole devilish thing. Now, there is nothing glorious about war, and what is the use of entertaining that stupid idea any longer? I know, as other members know, of returned broken and sick soldiers who have to support families although they are receiving no pension, not having applied in time. There are thousands of men who are now going around, wrecks of the last war, and there is no use saying that it is a glorious thing so far as they are concerned. Yet everyone who saw this spectacle in Montreal was stirred by it. I too might have been stirred by it, had I allowed myself to forget what it leads to, because military music does stir people; that is why they have it; otherwise men could not be induced to go into battle and kill one another.
It is rather interesting to look over this pamphlet, for which, I suppose, the country pays. On the front there is an advertisement of Molson's ale and on the back one of the Royal Bank of Canada, and between the two there is the military display. Let me give the names of some of the patrons of this peace spectacle which Montreal saw last Sunday: Their Excellencies; the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec; the Archbishop of Montreal; the Bishop of Montreal; the Premier of Quebec; the Minister of National Defence, otherwise known as the minister of peace; the Minister of Marine; the Secretary of State; the Mayor of Montreal; the Minister of Roads, Quebec; the Provincial Secretary; the Chief of General Staff; the Chief of Naval Staff-and a couple of other fellows. These are all peace people.
Did it include the member for Southeast Grey?

No, they missed me. Now, why can we not be out and out about this thing? Why can we not be absolutely honest? There are two schools of thought in Canada in regard to security. Both I believe are absolutely honest. One school believes that you will get security through military preparedness, and to that school the minister of this department belongs. He believes that if you prepare for war you will get peace.
I do not belong to that school. I belong to the school-and it is growing in Canada- which holds that if you want peace you must prepare for peace. And the methods where-
by peace is secured are not the same as the methods used to promote war. This peace sentiment is growing in Canada. I recall the time when some of us first tried to say things like this in the house, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself. When we made statements of this sort a gentleman, now a judge in the maritime provinces, shouted " bolshevik " and many other things like that. We were laughed to scorn; we were supposed to be fools who somehow or other by mistake had got into parliament. But to-day that attitude is not evident in the House of Commons; it is not seen to-night., although it is true there is a more or less empty house. Why? The answer is that after all parliament is but a reflection of the Canadian people and members dare not take that attitude. They were elected by the people and the people believe that war brings nothing but destruction and disaster not only, as the Secretary of State said the other day, to the vanquished but to the victors as well. War is an outgrown institution, as every advanced writer in every country agrees; and I do not know why in the world we cannot act on some of the best thought of the best people. For my part I would1 absolutely cut out every bit of national defence. The air force may be of some use at least in peace; it might be of some use in war, although I do not know. But certainly the other displays are of no use whatever, and when you come to items such as this the thing is simply vicious. It is a hypocritical attitude for the government to say and to expect any sane person to believe, that they are working for peace while at the same time they are poisoning the minds of the youth and making it impossible for these same youth, if they take training as cadets, seriously to promote peaceful ideas.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but there was one thing in connection with this parade in Montreal which is too good to miss. No doubt it was lovely as a pageant, but they concluded with the following words, sung to the accompaniment of massed bands: Abide with me; fast falls the eventide;
The darkness deepens; Lord with me abide; When other helpers fail, and comforts flee, Help of the helpless, O abide with me.
I fear no foe with Thee at hand to bless,
Ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness; Where is deaths sting? Where, grave, thy victory?
I triumph still, if Thou abide with me.
Was that not a wonderful thing to trail that in at the end of this glorious parade of military achievement? At least they held death up as the great ideal and aim of military preparedness.

I do not know whether the minister desires a discussion on the subject of defence; I do not know whether this is the proper time to bring it on. I doubt whether the committee is in the proper mood to go into the theme as thoroughly as the theme itself merits. But I find myself between two extremes to-night. On my right I find an hon. gentleman who holds, I believe, that some preparation will probably help to keep war off, although he thinks war is absolutely inevitable in all time to come. On my left are members who think war can be abolished and should be abolished, and that one way to abolish it is to stop making preparation for defence, and if necessary to throw away our arms and to declare to the world that we do not think we need fight any more.
I am between these two extreme points on the floor of this house to-night and I find myself having to take a more or less middle path philosophically. If I had to make a choice. I would not hesitate to line up with the hon. lady to my left. But I think I have a sound position, because the great philosopher Aristotle once took the same ground; he said that truth was to be found in the grand mean. And we have a more recent example in the Prime Minister and his party who have taken that position as between the extreme left and the extreme right; they say that they will go between the two, following truth in that path. If therefore I cannot get the ear of the minister in what I shall say to-night surely in view of the position I have adopted I ought to be acceptable pro tem at least.
First of all I want to pay the highest possible compliment to and express the deepest appreciation of the splendid idealism and sincerity of hon. members to my left who from time to time have stated, as they have done to-night, their absolute opposition to war in any shape or form, believing as they do, that we can get along without it; that we are more able to defend ourselves without the means of preparation than we are with them. I do not know whether or not they are correct in that position, but I do know they are doing a very great deal to stimulate the imagination of the people and create that will to peace without which peace on a permanent basis will never be achieved. In that great work I certainly congratulate them; I hope they will continue it and I hope they will be encouraged from every section to continue it. On the other hand, I want to say that I have no longer any allusions about the possibility of stopping war so suddenly, in
view of the actual conditions which I see in all parts of the modern world. While I think this idealism is admirable and necessary, nevertheless we cannot close our eyes to the great facts which scream at us from every section of the known world. I had the most profound admiration for the splendid fourteen points of the late President Wilson, but how far did they go? I think we would have to say that he overlooked the fundamental propositions, which were economic; those points, however sharp they were and however splendid, were absolutely doubled up and rendered useless by the economic forces with which they had to contend.
Therefore I submit that our consideration of this great problem of peace and war must extend, if it is to reach sound conclusions, to the real causes of war. I think the hon. members to my left who have emphasized peace as they have done, creating in the minds of the people of Canada a will for peace, will ultimately lead us to an understanding of the conditions which produce war and which make war absolutely inevitable. I know some people believe that Christianity can stop war; I think some hon. member mentioned that to-night. Obviously we have no Christians; that is the trouble. The only Christian of whom I ever heard was Jesus Christ himself; I never met another, never read of another, and do not believe there was ever another. We cannot stop war in that way; there are no Christians, so they cannot stop anything. Some people thought the international labour organizations could stop war. Until 1914 I had a profound faith in those organizations myself, but they did not stop war. Things went on as usual, and the very men who belonged to that international fraternity competed with each other in their mad rush to get at each others throats.
Then some say that if we get rid of our arms we will stop war. You might just as well tell me that the reason I do not hit the man sitting in front of me is because I have no arms. If you cut off my arms and I desired to hit him I would kick him; if you cut off my feet I would bite him ; no matter what you did I would find some means of attacking him. I do not think you can stop people from fighting even if you do not spend another penny on military preparations.
Save your money.

Yes, I think we might save it pro tem. I am not defending these expenditures; I am discussing the question academically. I do not think we can stop
Supply-National Defence

war by any idealism of that kind, nor do I think we can stop it by ceasing our preparations or by destroying the implements which for the moment we use in fighting. I think war goes deeper than that.
Let me say now, so that I shall not be misunderstood, that my antipathy to war is not less than that of the hon. member for Southeast Grey, nor is it less than that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I do not think war is a sensible thing; in fact I think it is a most impractical thing, but perhaps that is why it appeals to the house. I think we use the most impractical means possible in order to attain the most practical ends. War has no justification other than the fact that it is inevitable and that we do not know how to stop it; that is its justification. It has no moral justification; it has no economic justification; it has no human justification, but we do not know how to stop it, so we have to prepare for it. That is the position in which we find ourselves.
Now I wish to say one or two words further. I want to'suggest that a study of war, which perhaps every hon. member has made to some extent, must lead us to the conclusion that its chief cause is essentially economic. If that is true, if economic conditions cause war, the abolition of armaments will not stop it. If economic conditions cause war, the preaching of peace will not stop it, because you cannot reach economic conditions by talking about peace. So the only thing for us to do is to make a real, sincere attempt to go a little deeper than that and get at the economic causes. Let me suggest something along this line to the Minister of National Defence; I know he is against war just as much as the rest of us, but he finds himself in a position of responsibility. I also find myself in a position of equal responsibility, although I do not get the name for it; I am responsible for conditions just as much as he is, and I am not going to shirk my responsibilities. However, I want to make a suggestion to the minister, as a means of ultimately leading to that condition which hon. members to my left visualize for us so often. I think Canada to-day would be one of the first countries to be attacked; we have territory, and territory is what some of the nations of the world need most. If they go on breeding their populations at the present rate, they will have to have additional territory if they can get it by force. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked against whom we were preparing to defend ourselves; my reply is that we are preparing to defend ourselves against the first nation which so overruns its

own territory with its own population that it has to find additional space. I do not know which country that is going to be; I could name a few who are in a neck and neck race for the position, but that is one real cause.
Now I suggest to the minister that he endeavour to do a little good work along this line in connection with our immigration policy. I suggest that he get in contact with the Minister of Immigration, and that they say to Great Britain, "During the next thirty years we are prepared to take the surplus population which you now have provided that you will stop being an incubator for us. We do not want incubators. We will take your surplus provided you adopt a policy which hereafter will limit your population to your own resources." Just ask them to take an intelligent view of the question. Their population increases by about 400,000 every year; they have now a population of about 43,000,000, while they could not feed 25,000,000 on a high standard of living. What is the use of our taking the surplus population and relieving the pressure, while they keep on constantly increasing their population without knowing how they are going to feed them? That is a condition which leads inevitably to war. In addition to that, it is not an intelligent policy. I do not say Great Britain is the only country doing that; all Europe is in the same position, together with Japan, India and China, and we will be in a similar position some day if we follow this rigorous immigration policy now in force. I submit that if any farmer in western Canada tried to raise more pigs than he had swill for he would have the humane inspector at his door when that fact became known. However, the nations go on increasing their populations to such an extent that they scarcely have standing room for them. They say, "We must have no war," but the natural law steps in and says there must be war as long as nations blindly go on in disregard of the need to regulate population in relation to resources.
I suggest also to the minister that he use every possible effort to promote a policy which will lead to intelligent economic cooperation among the nations of the world. I think the Prime Minister, when he was speaking in reply to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) put the Situation correctly when he indicated that peace came about not by having any definite department to carry it into effect, but by the general policies for either peace or war which were carried into effect. That is just as true on this side of the argument. War will not come about by

having one department for defence, but it does come about by the general policy of all governments. So I would suigge&t that an outlook towards the economic co-operation of all countries of the world should be entertained as a general policy, internationally speaking, by the present government.
In the third place, we should continue to promote the ideal of good will amongst all the peoples of the world in a positive way, such as the hon. member for Southeast Grey never fails to do, and such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre never fails to promote.
In conclusion I want to suggest to the minister another thing which I have already brought to his attention through a resolution. In order that he might do the best with the money at his disposal, and in order that the preparations which we make may not incite to war but have the opposite effect. I urge that he follow the suggestion of the resolution which I brought before this parliament some time ago. I ask him now-not at some time in the future, not when war has broken out, but at this moment-to make -it known that should Canada foe led into future wars, immediately every agency that may be required for war purposes Shall be conscripted. I do not propose to repeat the argument I made when addressing the house on. that resolution, but I considered the minister's reply made on that occasion to be weak. I had not the opportunity at that time, but I now take the opportunity to tell him that I think it was weak. He said he was afraid to take such steps as the resolution referred to proposed- these may not be the exact words, but it is the idea-lest it should appear to other countries that we were trying to encourage war. Mr. Chairman, I think it would be a simple matter for the minister to get over that difficulty. If the Secretary of State were to indicate to all nations just what we were doing, and ask them to do the same thing, there would be no real doubt about our intention. I submit that the other countries would be more likely to think we were preparing for war if they happened to look at our estimates for this year and find that we have increased them enormously and taken no steps towards peace at all. If they knew that the Minister of National Defence had taken such a democratic and a fundamentallly better step than any other minister in the worid holding a similar portfolio, namely, to put the entire nation in the same position in the ease of war as the soldiers have been in all wars-placing them at the- command of the state-I tfhinlk it would make for peace.
I do not- think the Minister of National Defence can defend the attitude which we had to take in the last war. I do not think it was fair to have allowed a few men to control money during the war-men who by manipulation of credit or lack of intelligence to control it were the means of doubling the war debt of Canada. I do not think it can be justified that men who happened to be in Charge of factories manufacturing war munitions should be permitted to make enormous profits while soldiers died at $1.10 per day. I do not think the people of the next generation will stand for that kind of thing. If you want -to have a united Canada in the case Of a war coming upon us; if you want to have the very best type of preparation, now is the time to take the step to make it known everywhere that this is our policy. We do not want war with anybody, but if we have to fight we will all fight, and there will be no millionaires as a result, and mo special privileges as to those who Shall go and those who shall not go.

Suppose we come back to the consideration of the estimates of the Minister of National Defence. The hon. member who has just taken his seat mildly reproached the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodswor.th) and the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) for being idealistic.
No.

In his interesting but
somewhat rambling speech he has traced a pretty broad program for the government, as well as for parliament. I do not propose to follow him through all the ground that he has covered or explored, but there are two points I think are worth while considering.
He says that war is unjustifiable morally, economically, and in every respect, but that as it is unavoidable we must prepare for it. There was a time when it was said that plagues were unavoidable, and that the people had therefore to prepare to receive the plagues and* inter the victims-out of reach if possible- but that was all that could be done. If war is unjustifiable, then it behooves every parliament, every government, and every member of any representative body of the people, to try to find some practical means to prevent the evil of war reaching the country they are responsible for.
I do not propose to speak to-night on the doctrine of war or peace; I do not propose to consider the conditions of Europe and endeavour to find out whether there is likely to be a war in five or ten years. I simply desire the members of the government to consider

their responsibility to the people of Canada, in view of the attitude which most of their supporters took in the last election, and the previous one. Let them ask themselves if the attitude they take in this chamber, or in the country, outside of election .time, coincides with the position they took when they appealed to the people. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, I noticed that in the last four elections all the candidates of the Liberal party were elected on a peace program, and on a denunciation of the war spirit' and war policy of the Tory party. They made solemn pledges that they would endeavour to prevent the recurrence of any such thing as happened in 1914. They denounced the military expenditures of the Tory government and they promised to reduce those expenditures. The Liberal party is pledged to a peace policy and a reduction of military expenditure. I now ask the Liberal members of this house, as one of their free friends, to stand by their promises to the people of Canada, and especially to the people of the province of Quebec. That is one point.
The second point is: Is there anything in the international situation, so far as it concerns Canada, that justifies an increase in military expenditures? Has anything happened since 1917, or 1921, or 1925, to justify the Liberal party, brought to power under the conditions I have just mentioned, in increasing the military budget, under the pretence that we must keep in a state of preparation? Are the relations of Canada with any .country on earth such as to justify our taking that position? Does the position taken by our representatives at Washington, Geneva and London, justify our going on with war preparations? Does the intention already expressed by the Prime Minister, that we are prepared to adhere, as a nation, to the proposal of the American government for universal peace and arbitration, justify our increasing our military budget from what it was Jast year, after it had been increased last year over that of the preceding year? I say, no, no, from a moral point of view, with regard to the pledges given by almost every supporter of the government to the people who have sent him here. I say, no, with regard to the position which we have taken in international circles, in Geneva or elsewhere, as well as towards the United States of America. The geographical position of Canada is such that there is less risk for Canada in standing squarely for a peace and disarmament policy than there is, not merely for any other British country, but for any other country on earth; and more practical results are to be derived,
[Mr. Bourassa.l
not by mere verbal assertion, sanctimonious declarations of love for peace, while we bring in from year to year increasing estimates for war, but by proving in fact that what we say we mean; that we disarm, first, because we do not believe in war, and, second, because we do believe that the position which Canada occupies enables us to take that stand.
If you believe in preparedness, then I agree entirely with the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). If you believe in preparedness; if you believe it is the duty and the interest of Canada to prepare for any war emergency, then this military budget is a farce. If you believe in preparedness, as every country in Europe believed before the war and as some of them still believe, rightly or wrongly,-and I am not going to discuss to-night the policy of any country in Europe or elsewhere-then, do as do the countries that believe in a military policy. Know what preparedness is, and prepare seriously; but face the people of Canada honestly. Do not tell them at election time that you believe in peace and disarmament, and then come to parliament and say that you believe in a policy of preparedness. You cannot stand both for those who believe in a war policy and for those who believe in a peace policy. It must be one or the other. Neither this government nor any other can play with those feelings, those opinions, those principles. The hon. member for Southeast Grey and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are absolutely right when they say that the consciousness, intelligence and common sense of the people of this country are growing. Of course it is true there are still a number of people who believe in war and perhaps a larger number of people who believe in preparedness, although they hate war. I have no grudge against them; I respect their views; but you cannot be at the same time with those groups and with the other growing group who believe that Canada is so situated that a bold, courageous and practical policy for peace is the best move you can make at the present time in international affairs.
It was but this last fall that I went over all the western provinces, and some of my experiences there remain very vividly in my memory. I know the feelings of the people cannot be judged by one experience or two or ten experiences, but after all there is something in taking the pulse of the people in a most spontaneous way. I happened to address in Calgary a very large meeting, having regard to the conditions under which I spoke there. . It was in the midst of harvest; the season had been bad, nevertheless people

crowded in from thirty miles around to meet, not a man who had anything to offer to them, not a minister of the crown, nor a prospective minister, thank heaven! but just a simple individual who had been depicted to them for years and years by the press of all shades of opinion as an enemy of everything British, as a trouble maker, as the stormy petrel of the politics of Canada, who had been described to them more or less under the colours with which my good friend the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) covers me periodically. Nevertheless they came; and I thought I would make an experience. I delivered there the most antimilitaristic, anti-imperialistic, and some people would call it the most anti-British speech that I ever delivered in my life, a speech such as I never would and never did deliver in Quebec. I appealed to the sense of nationhood, the sense of racial fraternity, the sense of Canadian nationalism. Then I passed over the various causes of the last war, the arguments that had been used to justify us in going into the war, and later to justify us in adopting conscription. I did my best to show that all those features of our military policy before, during and since the war, were bad, were inimical to the. interests of Canada and really inimical to the true interests of the British Empire. I appealed especially to men who had been in the war and to their relatives; and the great consolation I had was, that after that meeting about fifty persons, veterans of the war, fathers and mothers of dead soldiers, with tears in their eyes, thinking of the boys who had sacrificed their lives because of the infernal propaganda carried on before the war to bring them into it, came and shook my hand and told me: "At last we have heard expressed what is in our bosoms and what has been in our thoughts for ten years. At last we find a public man who has the courage"-I repeat their language as it was-"to tell what we think". They had never dared say so because they would have been accused of lacking patriotism, of being untrue to their duty to the empire; but they began to realize that there is some other way of working for one's country and even for one's empire than by getting drunk with the wine of militarism, and fighting, and dying. There is living for one's country, working for one's country, endeavouring to increase by a useful life the moral and economic patrimony of all the races that inhabit Canada. Yes, the peace-loving sentiment is growing!
But there is more than that. Take our relations with the rest of the world. Let us
consider the situation of Canada, not as we imagine it but as it stands in the eyes either of the people of the United States or of the British people who know what it is. You hear it every time you go to London, every time you meet some of those clear-sighted men who know the real conditions of the British Emipire and of the world. Every one of them will tell you: Of course the case of Canada is entirely different from that of Australia and New Zealand. As regards Canada being obliged, even for imperial purposes, to make the same military expenditure as Australia and New Zealand, situated as they are on the border of the Asiatic continent, and having of necessity to rely upon outside help from a very distant country, your situation is so entirely different that the best service which you can render us is, so to speak, to wipe off from your political and international activities any possibility of your being a cause of war to England and the British Empire. Often, in the old chamber, I heard some of the most loyal leaders of the Tory party charge the British government with lack of love for or interest in Canadian affairs because they were always ready to disarm or to give way to United States pretensions and claims, disregarding our own claims and pretensions. I never could take that view. Opposed as I was, in those days especially, to the imperial policy followed in London, particularly under Tory governments, I always held and I repeat to-night that the best service England has rendered us has been precisely, after the war of 1812-14, to give way to the United States, because she realized that another war between the United States and England would be a piece of foolishness and a crime, and that Canada would be the sufferer by it. Those men who have a true sense of national pride, not the childish, not the noisy and cheap form of jingoism which can be put up so easily, but which we would have to put down so quickly in case we made good our childish provocations to the great nation to the south of us, those thoughtful men realize that a war between Great Britain and the United States, under all circumstances, would be a crime and a folly, and so long as Canada is connected with the British Empire, would be absolutely suicidal on our part. Therefore it would be true, and truer to-day than ever, that even if Great Britain were the victor in such a war, whether the British Empire was the victor or the vanquished, Canada would be the victim.
With regard to the rest of the world, what must logically follow, if the doctrine is held on the other side of the house that there is

You must be one or the other. Are you going to be a peace or a war government? Go to the people in that case and ask for a new mandate, because your present mandate does not

entitle you in honour to pursue a mild and weak war policy.

Will the hon.
gentleman allow me to make an inquiry, not in any spirit of challenging what he h'as just said, but because I would like to have the information? It is a general conviction which has been ingrained into our minds by the leaders of both parties for years and years. When for the first time we shared in an imperial war, in 1899, the only excuse given by the Liberal candidates in the province of Quebec was that the hands of Sir Wilfrid Laurier had been forced by Lord Minto and the Conservative party, and that if he had not given way the Tory party would have done much worse, whilst on the other side the Conservative party were denouncing Sir Wilfrid Laurier for having done what he did. In my constituency, for instance, I was fought by an official candidate of the Conservative party, who was supported by a very distinguished member of that party, a late minister of the crown in the province of Quebec, who accused me of being insincere because, having denounced the participation of Canada in the South African war, I did not go over to the Conservative party which he said would have done nothing of the kind. So that has been the atmosphere-and not only in the province of Quebec. If my hon. friend-I know he is a little younger than I am, and perhaps with his various literary pursuits he has not had the same time as I have had for reading old political records, and I do not blame him for not having the same tastes as myself-but if he would dig up the speeches that were made both in parliament and outside of parliament before confederation and after confederation by such men as Sir John A. Macdonald. Sir Alexander Campbell and the most
distinguished leaders of the Conservative party, he would find that they enunciated the very doctrine I have upheld this evening, that Canada is not obliged to participate in imperial wars. More than that, after confederation, Sir Alexander Campbell stated again in England, in the presence of all the representatives of the various Dominions and of the British government, that the pledge upon which confederation was made in 1865, as between the representatives of the imperial government and the representatives of United Canada, was that England, being the sole cause of possible wars for Canada, was morally obliged to stand by Canada in every war that could be declared by or against England and threaten Canada, but that Canada 'had no other duty than to defend her own territory. That was good Conservative doctrine for thirty years. I do not claim that hon. gentlemen opposite have not the right to renounce that doctrine, but I do claim that the people of Quebec, both Conservative and Liberal, have the right to stand behind that old policy. Similarly for many years they stood for the old, sane and moral policy of temperance as against the Yankee policy of prohibition, and they were denounced; but to-day their policy is being followed by the sister provinces, including the very moral province of Ontario. My hon. friend should remember the time when the province of Quebec was denounced for opposing conscription. I think, now the war fever has cooled, it is generally admitted that Quebec's opposition to conscription spared the lives of many of the youth of this country, not only in that province but outside, and that Quebec was no more criminal in taking that stand than were the people in Ireland, in Australia, in New Zealand and in South Africa, with the approval of the British government; that the people in Quebec were not necessarily the slackers and sluggards that they were depicted in the Tory press of Ontario because they chose to exercise1 their rights of citizenship in the same way as, for example, the Irish and the Australian people. There is a vote of $10,000 extra for the Royal Military College. The topographic survey has also made a strong case for an increase of 85,000 which, after consultation, I have agreed to put in the estimates. In connection with transport and freight, the vote has been absolutely too low and I have increased it to provide reasonably for an account which I must admit has been overdrawn in the matter of transport and freight largely for those going to camp.
These are the items in connection with which an increase is made. Let me assure the committee that these increases are not made in any militaristic spirit; they are not made because anyone here is glorifying war. I heard the remarks of my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), whose sincerity I respect, as I respect the sincerity of hon. members across the floor. But when I hear an hon. gentleman speaking of somebody coming forward-I think this was the expression he used-with a sanctimonious declaration of love for peace. I do not think it is quite fair to members of the house generally who have just as sincere a desire for peace as he has, notwithstanding what he may think. We have some responsibilities in this country as well as our desire for the idealistic. We realize that we are living in a world where we must keep our feet on the ground. I hope my hon. friend from Southeast Grey has accepted my apology-which I intended to make as abject as I could-but I want to assure her that this department is not being run with a view to bringing some personal glory to the minister or in order that the minister may make a success of it. My hon. friend might as well suggest that my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was anxious to encourage crime in order that the penitentiaries might be filled, so that his department would be magnified.

Is the minister apologizing
to the hon. member for Southeast Grey with regard to the statement that officers were not men?

I didn't say that; I
only asked, were they?

My hon. friend heard
what I said. I say, this department is not run in order to aggrandize the present minister. But it is necessary' that we should have a reasonable degree of efficiency. I do not agree with either the hon. member for Southeast Grey or the hon. member for Labelle, one of whom says that these expenditures are an absolute waste while the other suggests that the present provision is a farce. We are trying, on the best advice we can obtain and after consultation, not simply with military people but with those who take a deep interest in the defence of the country, to provide a reasonable service, to the end that we in Canada may hold up our heads and not only be prepared to defend our country but for another purpose which I am afraid some members of the committee do not realize is essential, namely, that we should be prepared to maintain our position as neutrals should the occasion arise. Because we happen to see a soldier on the street we need not conclude that we are going out to look for a fight. That is not the idea at all. The object is that we shall provide a reasonable force for defence and to maintain our neutrality if an emergency calls for it.
Now I should like to say just a word with regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from Southeast Grey referring to the military tournament at Montreal. I want to tell her that that tournament was not held at the expense of the department or the country in any way; I understand it was arranged by he officers and men of the Montreal militia units who gave a great deal of time and effort to it. I hope the hon. member was there; I would commend the show, if I may call it so, to anyone who would like to see good, clean, wholesome entertainment. I would commend it ahead of a good many other entertainments which were no doubt attended by respectable people in Montreal on that particular evening. If anyone wanted to see good gymnastic exhibitions, good drill and good equitation that was the place to go, and the good people of the city of Montreal did not seem to fear that their militaristic spirits would be unduly roused. I think the attendance the first night was 6,000 or 7,000; on the second night I understand 9,000 people were there, and on the third night the attendance was about 12,000.
Will the minister admit that was glorifying war just the same?

I am sorry, but I cannot admit that at all. I want to say that there are a good many members of this house who

have reasons for not glorifying war just as keen as those held by some of the hon. members who have spoken to-night. There is no attempt and no intention to glorify war, but there is some reason in this country for young men, having the idea that they have some duty to their country other than to simply get their living from it-
Is the minister inferring that those of us who talk as we have talked to-night are only here to get our living out of the country?
The minister is not inferring that at all, as I am sure my hon. friend knows.
That is what one would infer.

I am sorry my hon. friend took that inference, because there was no ground for it. I am only saying that a person is not necessarily glorifying war because he happens to put on a military uniform. While we have been carrying on military operations in a small way, I have not heard of very many Canadians who are anxious to go to war simply for love of it. I do not think that because you train a boy to use boxing gloves he is naturally going to become a pugilist or that he will be wanting to fight all the time. If we are going to adopt that sort of reasoning it seems to me that training in athletics or any kind of physical exercise is going to train the boy to use violence instead of the ordinary peaceful methods of life. I do not think there is much fear of producing that mental attitude simply because a man may happen to spend so many days in camp, or because he shoulders a rifle a few times.
Then I wish to say just a word with regard to this matter of peace and war and the conflicting policies suggested by my hon. friends, and I commend these remarks to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. For five, six, seven or eight years we have been talking disarmament; we have been working hard for it. When I say "we" I mean Canada; we are a member of the League of Nations, and the commissions of that league have been working with all their strength towards a position by which disarmament may be brought about. As yet that result has not been attained; I do not want to be discouraging or blue about it, but at the same time the prospects are not any too bright, judging from tihe last meeting of the preparatory conference on disarmament. But then along comes the United States with a proposition out of the blue, not that we should disarm but that we should become parties to a pact for 56103-2121
the renunciation of war. Does my hon. friend suggest that because the United States have taken that step they are inconsistent or hypocritical when, almost at the same moment, they increase their naval estimates by almost a quarter of a billion dollars? They realize that there is still a practical situation in the world.
May I ask the minister if the cutting down of the naval estimates so drastically was not quite in line with that very movement?

Perhaps it was, but I am only saying to my hon. friend that there does not seem to be any immediate prospect of disarmament, notwithstanding the fact that the United States is sincerely endeavouring to bring about peace. We are still in the world, and we have to remember that this utopian situation has not come about as yet. I do not want to take time to quote figures, but I think we have the smallest per capita expenditure in the world with regard to militia expenditures, and when we ask for a vote of S1.70 per capita, that should be compared with the per capita expenditure of France, which is $7.60; of Italy which is $6.11; of Japan, which is $3.91; of Germany, which is $2.60; of the United States, which is $5.07; of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, which is $13.03; of New Zealand, which is $3.07; of South Africa, which is $3.55 and of Australia, for which I have not the figure for this year, but which was $4.58 last year.

Has the minister the
figure for Denmark?
No; I am sorry, but I have not that figure. I submit that we are not travelling very fast along the road towards militarism when we request that amount.

May I ask if the
minister has the figures for the Scandinavian countries?
No, I have not.
Why give the figures for the militaristic countries instead of the figures for those countries which are striving for peace?

I should have thought,
from what I have heard, that Belgium is striving for peace; the United States is striving for peace, together with Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. I did hear that Russia was striving for peace, but I see that the per capita expenditure of that country is $3.06.

I wonder why the minister gives us that figure?
Because I notice it here, and Russia is a country which made a proposition only a short time ago for complete disarmament. At the same time, she spends $3.06 per capita on this account.
Then the minister is accusing Russia of insincerity because of that act?

I do not know what my hon. friend means by that. I will undertake to say that the actual expenditure is much more than the figure I have given, because Russia pays part of her military expenditures in kind which does not appear in dollars and cents at all.
Is not the minister accusing Russia of insincerity?

No. I say that a country which is held up before the world as one which proposes disarmament is herself spending $3.06 per capita on this account.
Progress reported.
